articles.title: Sen. Maria Cantwell warns of autonomous AI ‘swarms’ as she calls for federal guardrails
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Pointing to recent security incidents where networked AI agents spontaneously formed “swarms” to hack computer systems, U.S. Sen. Maria Cantwell (D-WA) took to the Senate floor Monday to demand urgent federal guardrails and mandatory independent safety testing for frontier AI models before their release.

Cantwell warned that recent security incidents involving autonomous AI agents executing unauthorized cyberattacks demonstrate that dangerous threats are already here, well before the arrival of superintelligence.

Citing recent public alarms sounded by tech leaders including Microsoft co-founder Bill Gates, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei, and OpenAI CEO Sam Altman, she emphasized that AI systems are advancing faster than expected and risk slipping out of human control without immediate oversight.

“The technology keeps advancing, the risks keep growing, and now the very dangers we’ve warned about — autonomous cyberattacks and biological weapons — are no longer theoretical,” Cantwell said. “We need our colleagues to say, ‘Stop with saying the industry can do what it wants’ and let’s put together the infrastructure at the federal level that not only has strong federal standards, but also has independent testing and real safeguards for the American people.”

Cantwell, a five-term senator and former RealNetworks vice president, delivered her speech in the wake of increasing alarm over rogue AI behavior and internal whistleblower warnings across the tech sector.
The senator highlighted several stark warnings during her address, pointing out that the risks associated with rapid AI deployment extend far beyond theoretical models:

On the speed and deceptive potential of agent networks: “These networks of agents are extremely well informed. They operate at the speed of light and, as we are learning, they are also capable of creating their own goals, and they are highly capable of deception.”

On why swarms pose a unique threat compared to standalone AI models: “Unlike powerful AI models designed to serve individual users… this situation with agents swarming is more difficult to manage and is far more dangerous.”

On Congress running out of time to establish federal oversight: “Now, some of these risks may not have been apparent in the last two years, but we would have stood up the muscle of our organization at the federal level to better detect risks like cyberattacks… At a time when we still had a window to get ahead of these dangers, the federal government, people here, were denying this opportunity.”

To address these emerging threats, Cantwell is calling on Congress to establish robust federal safety standards, independent third-party audit requirements, and dedicated federal infrastructure to evaluate advanced frontier models before they hit the market. Her legislative push centers on revival and passage of a suite of bipartisan bills:

The Future of AI Innovation Act: Originally introduced by Cantwell to empower the federal government to collaborate with industry to independently test advanced models for national security, biological, and cybersecurity risks.
The TEST AI Act and VET AI Act: Measures designed to bolster the Department of Energy’s testing capabilities for national security and establish official standards for third-party safety auditors.

A veteran policymaker on technology and innovation, Cantwell has long leaned on her private-sector tech experience to position herself as a primary legislative bridge between Washington, D.C., and the Pacific Northwest’s tech ecosystem.

As a lead author of the landmark 2022 CHIPS and Science Act, Cantwell helped direct federal investments toward AI and emerging technologies. Over her Senate career, she created the National AI Advisory Committee (NAIAC), championed small business adoption via the AI for Mainstreet Act, and led the opposition to a proposed 10-year moratorium on AI regulation.

articles.title: Goldman Sachs plants flag in Bellevue, opening hub for more than 125 AI and cloud engineers
articles.author: John Cook
paras: Goldman Sachs is expanding its technology presence in the Seattle region, opening a new Bellevue engineering center that will accommodate more than 125 employees focused on artificial intelligence and cloud transformation.
The New York-based financial giant held a ribbon-cutting ceremony this month for the new office, its first dedicated space for engineers in the Pacific Northwest.
The Bellevue location adds to Goldman Sachs’ existing presence in downtown Seattle, where the company has maintained an office since 2001 for its banking and wealth management divisions.

“We are in a period of rapid technological change, but we know our people are still this firm’s greatest asset,” Goldman Sachs Chairman and CEO David Solomon said in a statement. “Hiring exceptional talent is central to how we adapt and grow.”

Goldman Sachs employs more than 12,000 engineers globally, about one-quarter of its workforce. The company said the Bellevue office will give it access to the region’s deep pool of engineering talent and graduates from local universities.

The move also puts Goldman Sachs in the company of a growing list of financial and technology companies that have established engineering operations in the Seattle area. GeekWire maintains a list of nearly 150 engineering hubs in the Seattle region here .

JPMorgan Chase established its Seattle Tech Center in 2018 and has steadily expanded it. The engineering hub has grown to about 400 employees and is now anchoring a new AI infrastructure team focused on controlling how the bank runs AI across its own data centers and outside cloud providers.

Goldman Sachs said its new Bellevue location comes amid growth at other facilities in Dallas, Salt Lake City and Warsaw. Earlier this month, the company hired Dinesh Keswani — a former Microsoft and GoDaddy engineering leader — to co-lead its core engineering team alongside Gopi Parameswaran. Keswani will also serve as chief technology officer of The Core Engineering.

articles.title: Seattle’s Nuance Labs raises $50M to give AI models human expression and nuance
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: Nuance Labs , a Seattle-based artificial intelligence startup developing a foundational AI model designed to perceive and respond to real-time human expression, raised $50 million in Series A funding.

Founded in early 2025 by former Apple PhD researchers Fangchang Ma , Edward Zhang , and Karren Yang , the research lab is developing a single “full-duplex” foundation model designed to process and generate conversational cues simultaneously.

Unlike traditional setups that chain together separate tools for transcription, text generation, and voice or animation, Nuance’s model ingests live audiovisual signals like tone, gaze, and timing to stream real-time facial and vocal responses.
Existing avatars and voice tools fail because they force humans to adapt to the machine rather than the other way around, according to Ma, Nuance’s CEO.

“The most productive collaboration comes from being able to express yourself freely, in words, tone, gesture, and expression, the way you would with a friend or close colleague, with all the nuance in the back-and-forth that turns talking into understanding,” Ma said in a news release . “That’s what we’re building at Nuance Labs: AI that understands the many ways we express ourselves and responds the way a person does, in the moment.”

In a demo video accompanying the announcement (below), the startup showcased an avatar built to function as an active listener, adjusting its facial expressions and verbal cues dynamically as the user speaks.

Zhang, Nuance’s CTO, earned his PhD in computer graphics from the University of Washington and met Ma at Apple’s engineering office in Seattle. The two spoke to GeekWire last fall about building in Seattle rather than Silicon Valley and how they want Nuance “to be the premier research lab in Seattle.”

The startup plans to release a public research preview of its model later this year, giving users their first hands-on test of the interactive face-to-face avatar. Nuance targets applications where real-time human expression drives outcomes, including sales, customer service, professional coaching, and education.

Returning investor Lightspeed Venture Partners led the round, which also included participation from existing backers Accel and South Park Commons, alongside new investments from NVIDIA and Define Ventures.
The financing brings Nuance Labs’ total capital raised to $60 million following its $10 million seed round last year.

Nuance, which lists 24 employees on its website, plans to use the fresh capital to accelerate model development and hire researchers and engineers across modeling, data, evaluation, and real-time serving as it expands its team.

articles.title: Providence to receive $1.1B from Nike co-founder to build women’s health hospital in Oregon
articles.author: Lisa Stiffler
paras: Providence will receive $1.1 billion — one of the largest gifts ever pledged to a U.S. healthcare institution — from Nike co-founder Phil Knight and his wife, Penny. The donation will allow the nonprofit health network to build Oregon’s first hospital focused on women’s health, increase support for cardiovascular services and improve patient care.

“Penny and I have always believed that real breakthroughs come from people willing to take on the toughest challenges,” Phil Knight said in a statement. “Providence has shown that kind of ambition in cardiovascular care, and we see the same opportunity to do something truly distinctive for women’s health.”
The funds are being directed to Portland’s Providence St. Vincent Medical Center and to Providence Heart Institute.

The new women’s hospital will be located on the campus of the medical center and provide care in specialties including gynecology, pregnancy, labor and delivery, menopause and cardiovascular care. Providence leaders note that many pregnant patients are also managing hypertension, diabetes, behavioral health and substance abuse, requiring more specialized services.

The Knights have previously donated $200 million over the course of 10 years to Providence Heart Institute, which sees nearly 63,000 patients each year across the Pacific Northwest, up from 40,000 a decade ago. Cardiovascular disease is the leading cause of death and hospitalization in the U.S.
The added support for the institute will help pay for diagnostic cardiac imaging, additional clinical trials, and the recruitment of leading doctors.

Knight, 88, co-founded Nike with Bill Bowerman in Eugene, Ore., in 1964. The business was originally called Blue Ribbon Sports before rebranding seven years later. Knight is currently worth an estimated $25.4 billion, according to Forbes .

“The Knights’ extraordinary gift is a generational investment, leading to bold and innovative ideas that will shape healthcare in Oregon for decades to come,” said Jennifer Burrows, chief executive of Providence Oregon.

articles.title: America’s machinists are retiring, and two startup founders in their 20s want to salvage what they know
articles.author: Todd Bishop
paras: When machinists with decades of experience retire, everything they know about how metal behaves under a cutting tool — or anything else they learned through a career of scrapped parts and expensive mistakes — walks out the door with them.
A startup with roots in Seattle, started by two founders in their 20s, is building technology to capture that knowledge long before that point.
Neuramill , founded last year by CEO Nistha Mitra and COO Nick Khormaei , is developing what the company calls an intelligence layer for high-precision manufacturing.

The software reads a design file and figures out how the part should be made: which tools, which machines, and in what order. A machinist reviews and approves every plan before anything reaches the floor.

“This is a high-skill job, and nobody’s retaining this information,” Mitra said. When the machinists who know how to build complex jet engine parts retire, she said, that knowledge goes with them. “We help retain that for the future generation.”
Khormaei said the two founders spent much of the past year visiting machine shops to watch how the work gets done.
“The craft itself is so impressive,” he said. “They’re able to look at these drawings and models that come in and know exactly how to build it. It’s like they’re doing real-time physics simulation.”

Early customers and partners: The company says it has closed a six-figure contract with a major defense contractor, one of the companies known in the industry as primes. Neuramill declined to name the contractor.

Two of the machine shops using the software are Diamond Machine Works, a Seattle precision machining company founded in 1959, and VTN Manufacturing in San Jose, Calif. Satellite maker Astranis is a design partner.
Mitra said the company is not yet selling broadly, but has been paid by some of the early customers testing the software.

How they got here: Mitra, 26, has a computer science degree from the University of Maryland and spent three years at Oracle, most recently as an AI applied scientist in Seattle, working on multimodal models that reason across several kinds of data at once.

Khormaei, 24, holds bachelor’s and master’s degrees in electrical engineering from the University of Washington. He was a propulsion engineer at Boeing in Everett, where he worked on 777X fuel system electrical certification, and then spent part of last year at SpaceX as an integration and test engineer on Starlink manufacturing in Redmond.
He also grew up around machining. His father, Ron Khormaei, co-founded FINEX Cast Iron Cookware in Portland in 2012 and sold it to Lodge in 2019 . Khormaei worked production there as a teenager.

Where the software fits in: Neuramill’s technology works at a stage that has stayed largely manual: after the design file arrives, and before a programmer opens the computer-aided manufacturing (CAM) software that translates decisions into machine instructions.

Rather than position the company against Siemens and Mastercam, Mitra said Neuramill plugs into those systems. The company recently joined Siemens’ Frontier Partner Program, which gives startups access to the company’s software tools.
“At this point we are very collaborative with these companies,” she said, adding that the established vendors are looking for new technology of their own.

Bay Area and Seattle: Both founders worked in the Seattle region before leaving for San Francisco, a move Mitra described to GeekWire in February . They are back every four or five weeks now, working out of Foundations, the Seattle founder hub.
“We love this ecosystem. It gave birth to Neuramill,” Mitra said. They keep coming back in part for the customers: “This is a booming ecosystem in space and in aerospace.”
Funding and team: Neuramill has raised an undisclosed amount from Ascend, Breakwater Ventures, Schema Ventures, Creative Destruction Lab, Acequia Capital and Correlation Ventures.
The team is six people plus a contractor: the two founders, a chief research scientist who worked with Mitra at Oracle, and three engineers, one of them a machinist.

What’s next: The long-term goal, Mitra said, is a “world model” for manufacturing: a system that can reason across geometry, materials and machine behavior at any level of complexity. Even then, she sees a role for the people on the shop floor.

“There is a beauty to the craft of manufacturing that we should really respect,” she said. “There are some places where humans should not be extracted out of an industry, and I think manufacturing is one of them.”

articles.title: BuyWander raises $21M as retail returns startup expands nationwide from new Seattle HQ
articles.author: Kurt Schlosser
paras: BuyWander , an auction-based online marketplace for returned and overstocked retail items, announced Tuesday that it has raised $21 million in a Series A funding round led by Madrona Venture Group and Inspired Capital.

The fresh capital comes on the heels of the startup relocating its headquarters from Spokane, Wash., to the Seattle area to tap into the region’s deep pool of tech and retail talent and accelerate its nationwide warehouse expansion.
Founded in 2023 by CEO Jordan Allen and CFO Brock Kowalchuk , BuyWander connects bargain-seeking shoppers with inventory from major retailers like Amazon, Target, Walmart, and Home Depot.

Bidding on all items starts at $1 in fixed seven-day auctions, with customers picking up their winning purchases directly from local fulfillment centers to bypass shipping costs. The new funding — which brings total raised to date to $28 million — will fuel technology investments and power nationwide market expansion following recent warehouse launches in Denver and Chicago.

“This is blue ocean right now,” Allen said in an interview with GeekWire. “Nobody’s really built an incredibly strong consumer brand in this retail return space — what we call the intersection of the weird meets the wonderful underneath this misfit inventory. These items deserve a second chance, and as people have to tighten up their wallets, we’re an incredible option for them to buy the things they want and love.”

BuyWander officially relocated its corporate headquarters from Spokane to the Seattle area in August, establishing its central hub out of Kent, Wash., where 45 of its employees are based. The startup initially entered the region with a cramped facility to prove out local demand, but recently upgraded to a 52,000-square-foot warehouse that can process three to five times more volume for local shoppers.

Across its expanding national footprint — which now spans eight fulfillment locations — BuyWander’s total workforce has surged to 325 people, with the vast majority working in intake, stocking, and customer service.

“Spokane was a wonderful place to start the company,” Kowalchuk said. “It was where we were living at the time, and we were able to get a lot of feedback very iteratively. But getting to the size where we are today and building out that leadership team really requires a little bit more talent density that Seattle can provide with deep roots in retail and deep roots in tech.”
Allen previously founded Stay Alfred, a Spokane-based short-term rental company that shut down in 2020, amid the pandemic, after expanding to more than 30 cities.

Behind the scenes, AI is now helping BuyWander process and list hundreds of thousands of unique items each month. Historically, manual data entry and poor photography created a bottleneck for resale platforms. Today, automated tools instantly identify returned products, pull in retail valuations, and generate detailed listings with a single click.

“There’s been a ceiling on this business historically because of the technology required,” Allen said, adding that AI now optimizes everything from auction scheduling to appointment bookings. “It feels like World War II and Star Trek at the same time and we’re merging these two worlds together.”

To better capture regional markets, BuyWander plans to increase facility density in key metro areas. In the Puget Sound region, Allen noted that traffic and geography often create a barrier between regional hubs, pointing to plans to open four to five warehouses across the greater Seattle area over the next few years to keep pickup convenient for local shoppers.

Beyond bargain hunting, the circular model addresses a massive environmental headache for retailers, who often dispose of returned goods simply because their systems aren’t built to re-process them locally.

Total U.S. retail returns reach roughly $850 billion annually, driven heavily by online shopping, where return rates hover near 20%, according to data from the National Retail Federation and Happy Returns. For retailers, processing a single return can cost between 20% and 65% of the item’s original retail price once return shipping, inspection, and restocking are factored in — making local secondary marketplaces an increasingly vital alternative to taking a total loss.

“Some of these brands and retailers were throwing this stuff away, and it just feels kind of criminal,” Allen said, pointing out how returned items often get trucked back and forth across the country. “You can buy a Seahawks jersey, and it gets returned in the mail back to Hebron, Kentucky, and ends up loaded up on a truck, ending up in Miami. The stars really align when the stuff can be sold locally where the demand already was to begin with.”

BuyWander’s expansion is backed by rapid operational momentum, hitting 400% year-over-year growth as it expands nationally. The platform now counts 50,000 active and winning customers who have saved a cumulative $200 million — averaging roughly $4,000 in savings per customer. Over the past month alone, the company sold nearly 500,000 unique items across its eight warehouse locations, with goods selling for an average discount of 75% off retail prices.

According to Kowalchuk, roughly 80% of the returned goods arrive in “appears new” condition with only minor packaging damage. About 80% of buyers are end consumers using the platform for everyday shopping, while 20% are local resellers — a customer base Allen says grows almost entirely organically, with nine out of 10 shoppers joining via word-of-mouth referrals.

The platform offers a sprawling, unpredictable lineup of products — having sold everything from electronic cow milkers, log splitters, and commercial ice cream machines to everyday staples like hair dryers and air fryers.

“It is probably one of the best product discovery platforms out there,” Allen said, predicting the company will eventually sell a bit of everything listed on the internet. “We’ll get hilariously fun items, like foam blasters right after spring break or 12-foot tall skeletons right after Halloween. That’s why it’s odd, and that’s why the deals are so good.”

articles.title: Link Evening Closure Tuesday-Thursday
articles.author: Mike Orr
paras: The downtown tunnel will close early at 11 pm September 15-17 for planned maintenance. This is only in the evenings and won’t affect daytime service. The last Link trains through the tunnel each direction will be:

1 Line shuttle buses will run every 10-15 minutes between Capitol Hill and SODO stations. 2 Line shuttle buses will run every 10-15 minutes between Capitol Hill and Judkins Park stations. An earlier announcement said the shuttle buses would start earlier at 9pm, but Monday’s announcement doesn’t mention this,. so they may or may not start that early.
Check Sound Transit’s service alerts for the latest updates. A multilingual translation like is available at 800-823-9230 for passengers with limited English proficiency.
The reason for this is to extend Link’s after-hours maintenance period this month to make the system more resilient. I’m eager for Link to get more reliable someday so I’m glad for this maintenance.

articles.title: Bellevue Council Faces Decision Point on Parking Reform
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The Eastside's largest city is grappling with a new state mandate to scale back its off-street parking requirements for new development. In facing choices around going further than the new state-required baseline, Bellevue's leaders are facing crosswinds: a desire to continue reducing barriers to homebuilding is crashing into the city's car-oriented status quo.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

The new mandate is coming thanks to Senate Bill 5184 , a law approved last year that sets strict caps on the number of off-street parking stalls that Washington cities can require with new building projects. By next January, Bellevue will no longer be able to require more than one parking stall for every two apartment units, nor more than two parking stalls for every 1,000 square feet of commercial space.

The City will also be barred from requiring any parking for a broad set of uses, including apartments less than 1,200 square feet in size, commercial spaces that are less than 3,000 square feet, child care facilities, and affordable and senior housing.

The statewide parking reform is intended to ease cost burdens on builders, which are passed along to renters and homebuyers. Adding garage parking typically costs builders $60,000 per stall or more, according to the housing-focused Pacific Northwest think tank Sightline Institute.

Cities across the state are grappling with the new requirements, but Bellevue's size, prevalence of transit infrastructure, and positive trends in housing permit starts are putting a spotlight on how this new mandate gets implemented. Earlier this year, numerous councilmembers expressed clear interest in looking at how to be more ambitious in giving developers flexibility around parking, but recommendations that came out of Bellevue's planning commission hew much closer to the bare minimum.

A growing number of Washington cities are taking steps to fully eliminate parking mandates from their land use codes, following in the footsteps of places like Spokane , Port Townsend , and Bellingham . Vancouver abolished parking mandates as part of its Comprehensive Plan update earlier this year, with Tacoma next on deck. Next door to Bellevue in Issaquah, city leaders are considering eliminating mandates across a wide swath of the center city – an area where increasing housing growth is the goal.

A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue, no matter the studies showing the range of positive benefits that come from doing so. Earlier this year, UCLA's Institute of Transportation Studies published a new research synthesis looking at a range of studies considering the impact of arbitrary requirements to build parking and the quantified benefits that come from wiping them off the books.

"Across the research literature, scholars generally recommend eliminating minimum parking requirements. Removing these mandates lifts a major barrier to new housing and businesses, reduces the risk of parking oversupply, and encourages more efficient use of existing spaces," the researchers noted. "Slowing the growth of parking infrastructure can improve walkability and urban design, reduce environmental harms, and support more sustainable travel behavior."
A full repeal is likely a step too far for Bellevue officials, so instead the debate will focus on pulling a few additional levers.

"Considering that we have appropriately aggressive housing goals, and that many projects are struggling to move forward, I think we should continue to keep our foot on the gas. And I think there are some modifications we should consider to the final code, so that we can do that," Bellevue Deputy Mayor Dave Hamilton said last week.

By 2029, Bellevue will need to remove parking mandates from within a half-mile walk of light rail stations and within a quarter-mile of RapidRide bus stops. The city is going ahead and making that update now, but the council could expand that radius to a half-mile distance from RapidRide stations, which includes the B Line and the K Line , planned to open by 2030.

"Council has already established policy direction that we want more housing capacity near high-capacity transit, including allowing six units by right in a half mile of light rail and quarter mile of bus rapid transit [BRT], removing mandatory parking requirements in those areas that are transit served is consistent with the broader direction," Councilmember Vishal Bhargava said. "I would ask that we consider [...] the half mile around the BRT, and just as an analysis to see what the puts and takes would be towards that."
Naren Briar was the only councilmember to bring up the idea of a full repeal of parking mandates, laying down a potential marker for the future.

"I am personally interested in exploring citywide elimination of parking minimums. According to the research I did, cities like Austin, San Jose, Buffalo, had done this and seen a tremendous amount of economic boost as a result of that. So I do want us to, to be clear, I think if we did that now, it might cause a little bit of chaos," Briar said. "But I do want us eventually to see a city that is comprehensively integrated and allows end-to-end walkability as an effective mode of transportation for senior citizens, for young kids waiting at the bus stop, for for any resident or visitor of Bellevue."

Another issue likely to come up before a final vote in October is visitor parking. The draft code approved by the planning commission includes a set of requirements on top of the minimum required parking stalls for residential units, mandating every development with more than six units include one visitor stall for every 20 units. After 50 units or 20,000 square feet of gross floor area that requirement no longer applies, bizarrely.

"I'm inclined to think that our mandate should be eliminated, and I'm looking to Seattle and Redmond, where they don't have any visitor parking mandate," Hamilton said. "I think housing providers understand their customers' preferences and will build projects accordingly. This may be an area where we can follow the lead of neighboring cities and help ensure that folks who move here are not penalized."

There will also be a push in the other direction. At last Tuesday's meeting, a clear bloc formed in favor of sticking with the planning commission recommendation that included Jared Nieuwenhuis, Lynne Robinson, and Claire Sumadiwirya.

"Myself, I live in a townhouse community, so I would say if there's no visitor parking, somebody is not able to walk a half mile, take the light rail, then nobody's gonna ever visit me," Sumadiwirya said. "I have a lot of elderly friends, so I think it's really important to know that. I appreciate the take of meet the state minimum first. I think whenever there's something [that] changes in the policy, it's always good to be safe and finding that balance versus just I think making drastic, too bold changes that will be different."

Robinson, who served as Bellevue's mayor from 2020 to 2025, went even further than her colleagues and suggested that the city might make a push to amend state law to mandate parking at senior living facilities. She pushed back most strenuously on the idea of going further than the planning commission recommendation.

"Nobody's going to have service providers serve the seniors. Nobody's going to get a visitor, and Silver Glen is our only, I think, our only independent [living facility]," Robinson said. "I guess there's one next to Emerald Court, but independent senior living, and all those people have cars, and most of them cannot walk that far, so they're staying connected to the community by having the ability to drive, and if we take the parking away, it's going to really limit people's ability to live independently."

According to the National Resources Defense Council , 37.6% of Americans over the age of 75 have driving limitations, as of 2025. Nothing in the land use code would limit the ability for developers of senior and independent living facilities from building off-street parking with their projects – removing the mandate simply gets the city out of the business of deciding what's appropriate.
While not likely to represent a major sea change, the October 20 vote on parking reform will certainly signal what direction Bellevue is heading.

articles.title: Char the Chicken: Influencer chef and restaurant group ready to hatch new grill concept on Capitol Hill
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A growing Pacific Northwest incubator of restaurant chain concepts emphasizing health and sustainability is being joined by a celebrity chef for a high-profile poultry re-start on Capitol Hill.

The Conscious Hospitality Group is preparing the 11th Ave space formerly home to the flagship location of scuttled sustainable chicken sandwich concept Mt. Joy for a reboot as Char the Chicken , a “fire-grilled rotisserie chicken” concept that Instagram-famous Matt Broussard told the Seattle Times will overcome the challenging realities of the current Seattle dining economy because of his passion.
“Any other social media cook, they’re not gonna open a restaurant,” Broussard tells the Times. “Like, this is the dumbest thing you could do.”
The Conscious Hospitality Group backing will help.

CHG is a Bellevue-based restaurant collective and incubator led by co-founders Norman Wu and Danny Brawer . The company dedicated to “health, sustainability, and ethical business practices” pairs in-house concept development with operating partnerships, providing shared infrastructure, supply-chain scale, and administrative backing needed to expand sustainable, wellness-oriented food brands across the Pacific Northwest.

Privately held and so far free of institutional venture capital, CHG operates on an operator-funded growth-equity model. The company says it reinvests operating cash flows and savings from operational efficiencies from its high-volume, more mature concepts to self-fund earlier-stage ventures. The structure leverages buying power for things like certified sustainable proteins and 100% compostable packaging, while also reducing expansion risk as it tests new concepts.

CHG’s portfolio hits all the hours of the day, Its core expansion engine so far has been Just Poké while companion concepts like Sugo Hand Roll Bar and Hap’s Burgers adapt counter-service efficiency into urban sushi and comfort food. Complementing these are morning-to-midday wellness concepts like Sano Café and Matcha Magic , alongside low-overhead food hall testbeds like KODE Pizza, Club Seltzer, and EatDirt , which share prep logistics and validate experimental concepts before wider launches.

This framework played out on 11th Ave in March as the street’s Mt. Joy Chicken sandwich outlet suddenly shuttered ending long-term plans for aggressive expansion after a three-year run. Mt. Joy started with tech investor Robbie Cape’s plans to team up with prolific Capitol Hill and Seattle-wide restaurateur Ethan Stowell to launch Mt. Joy at 11th and Pine with the first of what they said they said would hatch into a 1,000 or more location chain focused solely on “pasture-raised” chicken. But early this year, CHG quietly pulled the plug.

Now with CHG executives on the paperwork, Broussard is the face of a new concept hoped to restore the 11th and Pine spot’s place in the restaurant group’s growing framework. The block is also home to another CHG brand, Matcha Magic, while the corner of 11th and Pine features the neighborhood’s location of Sweetgreen along with the salad chain’s “salad chutes” and “infinite kitchen” technology. Above rises the 2014-era preservation incentive-boosted Sunset Electric apartment building. The corner was famously at the center of the 2020 CHOP protests.

Broussard, known online as @acooknamedmatt , is a Texas-born, Seattle-based chef, cookbook author of Now We’re Cooking , and prominent food creator. After training at Le Cordon Bleu in Austin and working his way up through the Tom Douglas empire in Seattle, he gained a massive digital following during the pandemic with his energetic, ASMR-style videos and rapid knife work.
In media interviews earlier this year, Broussard said the new rotisserie chicken venture was hoped for a summer launch in time for Seattle’s host games during the FIFA World Cup .
Broussard tells the Times the Capitol Hill start of the Char the Chicken concept is now planned to launch in October.
Char the Chicken is opening at 1531 11th Ave. Follow @charthechicken for updates.

articles.title: Wilson slows homelessness plan including shelter goals in roll-out of 2027 budget proposal
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Belmont Village opened on Capitol Hill this summer

Mayor Katie Wilson is adjusting her homelessness plan , stretching out the timeline, funding mechanisms, and scope to bring more unhoused people indoors while managing an inherited $175 million budget deficit.

Saying her updated plan “doesn’t promise quick fixes that paper over real problems,” Wilson said this week the changes are part of her proposed budget that will be released next Tuesday, the first budget under the Wilson administration.

While Wilson’s core goals remain in place including the establishment of approximately 1,000 emergency shelter spaces paired with wraparound services, budget realities are going to slow things down. In March, the administration framed the delivery of 1,000 shelter units as a single-year objective for 2026. The September update extends that goal through the end of 2027, scheduling 960 total beds to serve an estimated 1,750 people annually across facilities established in 2026 and eight sites slated for 2027.

Fiscal and operational costs have also grown. The updated plan directs $37 million toward shelter capacity and allocates $11.2 million in 2027 toward rental assistance, eviction prevention, and legal aid. The approach places greater emphasis on acute care, citing King County survey data showing 33% of unhoused individuals experience substance use disorders and 27% report serious mental illness. The plan also incorporates the return of homelessness contracting to the city from the King County Regional Homelessness Authority .
Addressing the deficit challenges, Wilson said her updated homelessness plan will rely on existing revenues redirected within the upcoming 2027–2028 budget.

Despite an executive order in the early weeks of her administration and the launch of a new Tiny House Village-focused strategy this spring, Wilson has made only slow progress on increasing the city’s shelter capacity. While Belmont Village opened with 31 new shelter homes on Capitol Hill in July , Wilson’s acceleration plan has produced only 75 additional new units at a new village in Interbay.

articles.title: Mayor Katie Wilson Presents Gun Violence Prevention Plan
articles.author: Guy Oron
paras: Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson is rolling out a plan to tackle gun violence by better integrating city departments and maintaining services for youth. The announcement comes after weeks of relentless criticism of the city’s public safety track record by local corporate media and a slew of big businesses following the Bite of Seattle mass shooting in July.

Flanked by Seattle Police Department (SPD) Interim Chief Andre Sayles and CARE Department Chief Amy Barden, Wilson sat down with The Stranger and explained that the city had to do more to break down silos between the two public safety agencies.

As part of the plan, the CARE Department , which operates Seattle’s 911 call center and a team of 40 non-police crisis responders, is being given a bigger role. Wilson’s budget proposal will keep the department’s gun violence director and fund an additional gun violence coordinator. The department is also taking over nine contracts with nonprofits—worth about $5 million annually—to do violence interruption work for the city.
Barden says transferring the contracts will enable CARE department responders to quickly know when a young person in crisis has already been working with a case manager or mentor.

One obstacle to the CARE Department’s success has been the City’s labor contract with the Seattle Police Officers Guild (SPOG), which represents rank-and-file cops. In August, Seattle’s Office of the Inspector General released a report claiming that the CARE department’s “scope of work remains significantly impacted” by the SPOG contract, which requires all 911 calls to be routed through a dual dispatch system that includes SPD officers.

Barden rejected the idea that the SPOG contract could throw a wrench in Wilson’s gun violence plan, saying “the contracts really don’t matter as long as the first responders know how to hand off to each other.”

Barden cited internal data suggesting that over the last six weeks, the CARE Department’s responder utilization rate has gone up to 80 percent as cops are diverting more cases. Last year during the same time, the team was only utilizing about 40 percent of its capacity, CARE Department spokesperson Bobbie Nickel says.

A large part of this could be due to the department’s expansion in early August, which broadened the crisis response window to 18 hours a day and nearly doubled its force. The growth was funded by a recent 0.1 percent sales tax hike .

Sayles said that under his leadership SPD management has been pushing rank-and-file officers to divert more calls to the CARE Department and clear up misinformation about the limitations of the SPOG contract. Sayles was deputy chief at SPD for a year and has been the acting police chief for seven weeks.

“Our supervisors [are] really diving into it and making those connections, understanding that we have a lot of work that we do on a daily basis as police officers, and saying this isn’t our wheelhouse,” Sayles says.

Wilson also pledged to increase SPD foot and cyclist patrols in Belltown, Little Saigon, Rainier Beach, and along Aurora Avenue North. She said this is the first step of a “focused deterrence” approach, which is essentially a carrot and stick strategy where punishment is paired with offers of services and diversion.

On top of the CARE team capacity changes, Wilson believes youth services can help ameliorate rising gun violence. The upcoming budget conversation will be difficult—the city is facing a $175 million budget deficit. But Wilson maintained she will shield funding for youth services. That includes maintaining mental health care investments and allocating $600,000 for a new after school program in Rainier Beach, plus keeping open a ninth Teen Late Night center in West Seattle.

The City is also partnering with the University of Washington and John Hopkins University to review its gun violence prevention strategies and develop a new review process to analyze every homicide. Some city council members would like to see the City pursue different partnerships, though.

Seattle City Councilmember Martiza Rivera has introduced a resolution asking the City to adopt that model and partner with the National Network for Safer Communities. Consulting with the organization could cost the city more than $400,000 .

Embarrassingly, at a September 8 Public Safety Committee meeting discussing the resolution, Rivera mixed up Seattle’s shots fired and homicide statistics, inflating the latter count by “an order of magnitude ,” as Publicola reported. Since 2024, homicides in Seattle have been trending downward. In the first eight months of 2026, the City had five fewer homicides compared to the same period in 2025, a 23 percent decrease.

Wilson said the City was already working on a focused deterrence strategy, and that, although she shared the same goals as the council member, Rivera “has a little bit of a different idea for how to get there.”
Ultimately, Wilson says although there is no “magic solution” to gun violence, her collection of strategies could bring down the numbers further.
“We are making progress—gun violence is down—and [yet] there is no acceptable level of violence,” Wilson says.

articles.title: Pittsburgh’s kindergartners fall below the measles safety threshold, testing the city’s vaccine legacy
articles.author:
<name>Rebecca Smullin Dawson, Associate Professor of Biology, Allegheny College</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/rebecca-smullin-dawson-1436960"/>
paras: It takes a lot to knock football out of the headlines in Pittsburgh. But reports of measles cases , exposure alerts and calls for residents to double-check their vaccination status have dominated local news since August 2026.

My office at Allegheny College, where I am an epidemiologist , is within a few steps of a classroom dedicated to Dr. Thomas Francis . Dr. Francis also coordinated the entire polio vaccine field trial, which included 1.8 million children, and deemed the polio vaccine “ safe, effective, potent .”

As of Sept. 14, 2026, the Pennsylvania Department of Health has confirmed 693 measles cases across 38 of the state’s 67 counties this year, including 133 hospitalizations and three deaths among unvaccinated residents . That compares with 16 cases statewide in all of 2025.

Allegheny County reported its first case tied to the current outbreak in August, when the county health department warned of a potential exposure at UPMC Children’s Hospital’s emergency department. Two confirmed cases were diagnosed on Aug. 27, 2026, but the patients left the county afterward.

Pittsburgh is where Dr. Jonas Salk developed the first polio vaccine on the campus of the University of Pittsburgh. Children throughout the Pittsburgh area , including my father, lined up to participate in the Salk vaccine trials in 1954.
That history offers a useful lens for understanding today’s measles outbreak: what’s driving it, how it spreads, and what residents in the Pittsburgh area need to know.

Measles is one of the oldest and most contagious diseases. In fact, measles was around when the Egyptian pyramids were being built . Archaeological evidence shows the measles virus in the Tigris and Euphrates river valley in 3000 B.C.E .

Measles is an acute respiratory virus. If an unvaccinated individual who has never had measles is exposed to the measles virus, they will likely become sick. Measles easily spreads through the air. Infected individuals are contagious 3-5 days before symptoms occur, a transmission mechanism known as asymptomatic spread. Viral particles remain active and infectious for up to two hours after a person with measles leaves a room.

Symptoms of measles include a fever as high as 105 degrees Fahrenheit, cough, runny nose, conjunctivitis and Koplik spots , which are small white or bluish-white spots that appear on the inside of the cheeks before the measles rash breaks out on the skin. These spots are the defining diagnostic feature of measles . Measles also results in a rash, known as a “bucket of paint rash” because it looks like someone spilled a bucket of red paint over the head of the sick person.
The rash is not contagious. This disease spreads when someone breathes in the virus.
Before there was a vaccine for measles, upward of 3 million people – mostly children – were infected in the U.S. each year, 48,000 were hospitalized, and as many as 500 died .

Measles was eliminated in the United States through vaccination in 2000 , meaning person-to-person spread of the disease was disrupted. However, due to declining vaccination rates , measles is once again spreading throughout Pennsylvania, resulting in approximately four times as many measles cases in 2026 within the state as in the previous 30 years combined.

Measles vaccination rates need to be above 95% to prevent the disease from spreading. The current outbreak has affected a majority of Pennsylvania’s 67 counties , an indicator that even small declines in vaccination coverage result in large outbreaks.

The MMR vaccine is covered at no cost by most private insurance plans and is available free of charge to Medicaid-insured, uninsured or underinsured children at any of Pennsylvania’s 59 state health centers . The American Academy of Pediatrics recommends children receive two doses by ages 4 to 6 to ensure protection against measles.

Allegheny County’s kindergarten MMR vaccination rate was 91.8% for the 2025-26 school year – below the 95% threshold needed to stop measles from spreading and part of a decline the county health department has tracked for more than a decade .

If you are vaccinated or have had measles, there is little risk – about 3% – that you will develop measles if exposed to the virus. There is no need to quarantine, but even vaccinated people should watch for symptoms of disease.

For people who are unvaccinated, including infants, the risk of developing a measles infection after exposure is approximately 90% . Unvaccinated individuals need to quarantine. Local health departments require them to stay away from others for 21 days to prevent the asymptomatic spread of disease.
If an individual in quarantine becomes ill, they will begin a minimum 14-day isolation.

Measles is a serious disease. Approximately 20% of people who get it will develop pneumonia; many will require hospitalization, and a few will die. Each measles case costs our healthcare system approximately US$43,000 , according to a Johns Hopkins systematic review of outbreaks in 18 states.

The measles virus also has the ability to suppress one’s immune system . This means that after a bout of measles, survivors can be left more vulnerable to other infections they were previously protected against, sometimes for months or even years afterward.

In order to prevent measles from spreading in our communities , at least 95% of the population must be vaccinated. The MMR vaccine was designed to prevent an individual from developing measles. But there is an added bonus: When the majority of a population is vaccinated, there are community-wide effects, mainly that community transmission of measles will begin to decline.
Pittsburgh helped end one vaccine-preventable epidemic 70 years ago. The current measles outbreak could be a test of whether the local history still means something for vaccination rates today.

articles.title: Middle East is the latest arena of political recalibration for Italy’s right-wing but pragmatic Meloni
articles.author:
<name>Julia Khrebtan-Hörhager, Professor of Critical Cultural & International Studies, Colorado State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/julia-khrebtan-horhager-1327191"/>
paras: Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni has made a political art of being many things at once.

Since coming to power in 2022, she has become the leader of Italy’s longest-serving postwar government. Meloni has also transformed herself from a politician once viewed as a radical outsider into one of Europe’s most consequential conservative leaders . Her political strength has always rested on adaptability: whether speaking the culture war language of MAGA politics in Washington, European pragmatism in Brussels or nationalism in Rome.
Nowhere is that adaptability more visible than in her dealings in the Middle East.

Her government has long cultivated close relations with Israel and presented itself as one of Israel’s strongest political supporters in Europe . This position was in part self-serving for Meloni: As a leader of a party with roots in Italy’s post-fascist right , the approach to Israel – alongside repeated condemnations of anti-Semitism and the racial laws of the fascist regime – signaled a break with the past.

Yet her strong support for Israel was increasingly at odds with public opinion at home, which moved sharply against Israel as the war in Gaza ground on. Some 75% of Italians hold an unfavorable view of Israel, up from 66% in 2025, according to a June 2026 Pew Research Center survey .

Perhaps recognizing the yearslong shift, Meloni subtly changed course. In April 2026, Italy suspended the automatic renewal of its defense cooperation agreement with Israel. That followed growing public criticism of Israeli military actions in Gaza and Lebanon, including an incident in which Israeli forces fired warning shots at a clearly marked Italian U.N. convoy in southern Lebanon, damaging one vehicle but causing no injuries .

It was the kind of symbolic recalibration that Meloni has increasingly used to position Italy as a geopolitical hinge between competing power centers in order to maximize Rome’s room for maneuver on the world stage. The Middle East has just given that strategy a new environment.
None of that is to suggest that Meloni has in any way become an anti-Israel leader.

Diplomatically symbolic as it might have been, suspending the renewal of the defense cooperation agreement had almost no practical effect on Israel. Notwithstanding that and other occasional disagreements over things such Israeli settlement activity , the two countries maintain close diplomatic and economic relations.

Italy, moreover, has been a reliable backer of Israel in international forums in the course of the war in Gaza. And notably, Italy declined to join the U.K. and France in banning goods from the occupied West Bank – an issue that has driven a wedge between EU members and Israel – though Italian Foreign Minister Antonio Tajani has said Rome is considering such measures .

Instead, Meloni’s rhetoric on Israel appears to represent primarily a form of political and reputational management rather than a substantive policy shift. Yet it shows how Meloni is particularly receptive to political realities and looking for ways to make the case for Italy as a useful diplomatic partner that talks to all sides.
And here, Lebanon offers another clear example of her approach.

In August 2026, Meloni hosted Lebanese President Joseph Aoun for discussions largely focused on the political and military situation in southern Lebanon, continuing Israeli attacks and the future of UNIFIL , the U.N. peacekeeping mission in which Italy has the second-largest contingent – and the most of any European country. Rome likewise hosted the latest rounds of direct talks between the Israeli and Lebanese delegations.

The diplomacy is part of a yearslong Italian involvement in Lebanon. Beyond its support for UNIFIL , Italy also trains Lebanese security forces and has maintained a significant diplomatic presence in the country. As UNIFIL’s mandate approaches its scheduled end on Dec. 31, 2026 , Italy is also working with France and other partners on what might replace it and how to avoid a security vacuum.
In Lebanon, Italy has an established presence on the ground dating back years, a relationship with Israel, and the ability to speak to Washington and European allies .
Aoun’s government has a reason to want Italy involved, but that role also creates a dilemma for Meloni.

On Sept. 6, 2026, Israeli strikes in southern Lebanon killed several people, according to Lebanese authorities , prompting Aoun to condemn what he called a dangerous escalation and appeal for international intervention. Israel said it was responding to Hezbollah attacks and was targeting the militant group’s infrastructure.

Lebanese leaders won’t see Italy as a credible interlocutor if it ignores Israeli violations of a June 2026 ceasefire . At the same time, Meloni cannot simply abandon Israel without damaging a relationship that she has spent years cultivating.

Yet for Meloni, Italy’s ability to maintain relationships with opposing sides provides diplomatic value, even if the process ultimately does not lead anywhere. Her approach is therefore best understood as one of political calibration: acknowledging concerns over Lebanese and Palestinian suffering, while preserving Italy’s relationship with Israel and maintaining diplomatic access to competing sides.
There is another reason Italy is becoming more active in the region: economics.
The Mediterranean is not simply Italy’s geographical neighborhood. It is a strategic economic space involving energy, trade, infrastructure, investment, migration and security.
Italy’s ties with the Gulf are not new , but Meloni’s government has stepped them up, giving economic and strategic interests a more prominent role.

The previous government was already seeking closer ties with Saudi Arabia. Under Meloni, the relationship has gone further. In January 2025, Italy and Saudi Arabia upgraded their ties to a strategic partnership and signed agreements worth around US$10 billion.

By 2026, Foreign Minister Tajani was describing the Saudi relationship as “ one of the pillars” of Italy’s regional engagement . He has explicitly linked it to political, economic and security interests, including the protection of maritime routes through the Strait of Hormuz and the Red Sea.

The scale of this economic relationship is also becoming clearer . Italian exports to Saudi Arabia reached around $7.2 billion in 2024, up 28% from the previous year, with Italian companies looking to take part in Saudi Arabia’s Vision 2030 projects in areas such as infrastructure, transport, technology, energy and tourism.

The United Arab Emirates is another important market : Italian exports reached about $9.2 billion in 2024, up 21%. And during Meloni’s February 2025 visit, the UAE announced plans to invest $40 billion in Italy and signed more than 40 agreements covering areas including investment, energy, defense, space and technology.
The Gulf is therefore becoming more than an energy supplier or diplomatic partner for Italy. It is an increasingly important market for Italian exports, investment and business.

This economic dimension helps explain why Italy’s regional activism under Meloni is best understood not as a wholesale departure from previous governments but as a pragmatic intensification of a long-standing strategy of diversification , commercial diplomacy and strategic flexibility.

For Rome, stability in places such as Lebanon matters not only because of humanitarian and security concerns. Even though Italy’s direct economic exposure to Lebanon is comparatively limited, the Meloni government views Lebanese stability within a wider regional framework in which conflict can affect maritime security, energy markets, trade and investment.
Meloni has sought to convert Italy’s geographical position and existing relationships into economic and diplomatic leverage, while preserving room to engage with a wide range of regional actors.

This is consistent with a broader pattern in Italian foreign policy under Meloni: less a commitment to fixed ideological positions than a persistent effort to preserve room for maneuver. The Middle East now offers a particularly revealing test of that strategy.

articles.title: We paid college students about $5 a night to sleep at least 7 hours – and their grades quickly improved
articles.author:
<name>Osea Giuntella, Associate Professor of Economics, University of Pittsburgh</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/osea-giuntella-1373960"/>
paras: Paying college students about US$5 a night to sleep seven hours got them a quarter more nights of adequate sleep – and better grades.
That is what we found in a study we published in July 2026 .

We gave more than 1,100 undergraduates at University of Pittsburgh a Fitbit – a wearable activity tracker that looks similar to a watch – and an app that sent bedtime reminders and morning feedback. We randomly chose 468 students and paid them about $5 for every night they slept at least seven hours, over the course of four weeks. We verified how much they slept using the device they wore.
The students were about 19 years old, on average, and half of them were first-year students. Roughly 72% of them were women. About 55% were white, 28% Asian, 9% Black and 4% Hispanic.
Our study shows that offering an immediate financial reward can help students meet a seven-hour sleep goal, and that those effects can persist up to a month beyond when the students are paid.

About one-third of American adults sleep less than seven hours a night, and a similar share say they wish they slept more. Among adolescents and young adults, roughly two-thirds routinely fall short of getting seven hours of sleep a night – the amount of shut-eye that health authorities recommend .
One prominent sleep researcher has called sleep deprivation the most prevalent high-risk behavior.
Short sleep is linked to obesity, diabetes, high blood pressure, heart disease, stroke and early death .
Irregular sleep predicts mortality risk even more than sleep duration does . Sleep loss shows up in decision-making, even when it comes to issues like whether people vote .
Before we changed anything, the average student in our study slept 6.6 hours a night .
Half were going to bed after 1 a.m. on average – a quarter after 2 a.m.
Students got the recommended seven hours of sleep on a typical weeknight on only 43% of their nights, and more than 85% fell short at least once a week.

They also did not know how much sleep they were getting. Two-thirds told us they usually slept seven hours – the trackers showed only about one-third of students slept that much on even three nights out of five.
And 94% said their ideal night of sleep was longer than the one they were getting.

The 468 students we offered nightly payments reached seven hours of sleep on 26% more nights than 380 students who were not offered the money. That is a large shift for a group in which fewer than half were hitting the mark to begin with.
Students receiving the monetary incentive slept 19 more minutes per school night, roughly the difference between closing the laptop at 11:40 p.m. or at midnight.

Among students receiving the payment incentive, their GPA rose by about 0.08 points that semester – roughly a quarter of the gap between students who arrived with above-average and below-average high school grades.

Once the payments stopped after four weeks, students who had received the money were still sleeping about eight minutes longer per night for the remaining three to four weeks of the study. The effect was smaller than during our study, but our findings suggest that some of the change in sleep habits persisted for up to a month after the end of the incentive.
The effects of the intervention on sleep and GPA were largest among first-term freshmen, whose routines are not yet necessarily fixed.
Timing mattered too: Delivering the payment as a lump sum at the end of the semester, rather than every morning, produced only about two-thirds of the effect on sleep.
The effects of the intervention on GPA faded over a couple of academic terms. Grades remained higher in the following semester, but two semesters later we could no longer detect an effect.

Bedtime reminders and morning feedback on their own – with no money attached – had little effect. Students who received them slept only marginally more. The problem was not motivation: Nearly all said they wanted more sleep than they were getting. The challenge was following through on that intention night after night.
Our results show that universities should look at how the environment they create fosters or discourages good sleep habits.

Late evening deadlines to submit assignments and early classes can both make it harder for students to get enough sleep. Changing some of these features costs little compared with many academic support programs, and it may be worth testing alongside other interventions aimed directly at students.
Reminders and feedback might also work better if they change over time, rather than becoming familiar and easy to tune out.

Very few universities or students treat sleep as part of an investment in education, or ask whether the schedules and incentives schools create make adequate sleep harder. Our results suggest they should.
