articles.title: How libraries in Philadelphia, Pittsburgh and other Pennsylvania communities evolved from subscription clubs to vital public institutions
articles.author:
<name>Bernadette A. Lear, Education, Behavioral Sciences, and Social Sciences Librarian, Penn State</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/bernadette-a-lear-2726979"/>
paras: As a librarian who researches and writes about library history in Pennsylvania , I was delighted to see the American Library Association’s efforts to celebrate its 150th anniversary this year, while making several mentions of Pennsylvania.

The ALA highlighted its 1876 founding in Philadelphia ; how Pittsburgh philanthropist Andrew Carnegie funded the construction of more than 1,600 library buildings throughout the United States; and Scranton’s Henry and Edith Carr , who attended and maintained records about the ALA’s early conferences for nearly 50 years.
But these stories just scratch the surface of how Pennsylvanians have contributed to American libraries and librarianship.

I published a book on Pennsylvania libraries from the 1700s through the 1940s , and I’m working on a sequel that extends the story to the early 2000s. Many scholars connect the beginning of public librarianship in the United States to ALA’s 1876 founding, but libraries’ roots go back much further .
The Library Company of Philadelphia , established in 1731 by Benjamin Franklin, was the nation’s first successful circulating library and was a model for many others.

These early “public” libraries – so called because they did not require users to affiliate with churches, colleges or other organizations – were run by stockholders who pooled funds to purchase books. The owners charged annual membership fees to others who wanted to join.

In the 19th century there was widespread desire among U.S. educators, women’s clubs, local government leaders and public-spirited citizens to provide libraries to everyone, whether or not they could afford to subscribe.
Today, some people incorrectly believe that steel magnate Carnegie was the first philanthropist to donate money for library buildings. However, a number of other Pennsylvanians preceded him.

In 1883, for example, Thomas Struthers , a lawyer and land developer, constructed a multipurpose building in Warren, Penn., that contained a theater and storefronts. Those spaces were to support a public library that was also in the building. The business plan didn’t work, however, and users had to purchase “tickets” to borrow books.
Given such situations, Carnegie’s philanthropy was especially impactful because it shifted some financial responsibility to local governments.

While some of the lavish libraries Carnegie first erected in the Pittsburgh area came with endowments – the Homestead library is one that still exists – he later developed a formula to ensure that other communities would not rely on his continuous generosity. As a condition of most of his grants, Carnegie insisted that municipalities provide land plus annual operating funds equivalent to at least 10% of the buildings’ costs. This effectively committed municipalities to finance libraries with public dollars.
In Pennsylvania, rural residents received a library boost with the passage of Act 329 in 1931. The legislation offered partial matching funds to counties that provided library services.
Notably, the law excluded the state’s two largest counties – Philadelphia and Allegheny.

The federal Library Services Act of 1956-1962, a forerunner of the current Grants to States program, further aided libraries in communities with fewer than 10,000 inhabitants. The funds supported book purchases and projects such as bookmobile services.
Until the 1960s, though, there were no parallel funding streams for larger communities. This may have compounded other inequities.

Pennsylvania libraries did not practice de jure racial discrimination as Southern libraries did . Nor did they deliberately exclude senior citizens or people with disabilities. But how they allocated resources, designed spaces, developed collections, recruited staff and engaged local residents through specialized programming favored some constituents over others.

Just a few weeks ago I uncovered a November 1969 article in the Pennsylvania Library Association bulletin that was written by Augusta A. “Gussie” Clark , once a librarian and later a member of Philadelphia’s City Council. Clark wrote about how she believed white librarians in the City of Brotherly Love were failing Black children. She described the librarians’ lack of respect for Black communities, their “pained tolerance” of Black people in their midst, and an unwillingness to render extra help – all of which, she said, prevented Black children from feeling “at home” in public libraries.

Using libraries’ records, I have also found many requests from both individuals and advocacy groups asking for ramps, elevators and other alterations to century-old libraries, and for additional listening and viewing equipment. In at least one case, a complaint reached the U.S. Department of Education’s Office for Civil Rights; it was investigated and ultimately dismissed.

Libraries in urban areas of Pennsylvania began to receive state support after the passage of Act 188 of 1961, which created a state aid program for municipal as well as county libraries. It also provided additional funding to the Free Library of Philadelphia and Carnegie Library of Pittsburgh, which became Statewide Library Resource Centers. As such, they received extra funding to provide services to other libraries and customers in the state.

On the national level, the Library Services and Construction Act , which replaced the Library Services Act in 1964, did not exclude urban and populous suburban areas as the Library Services Act had. In administering the new funds, the State Library of Pennsylvania approved many proposals that extended services to underserved residents, such as Montgomery County-Norristown Public Library’s outreach to public housing complexes and prisons , Altoona Area Public Library’s L.I.F.E. program for people with intellectual disabilities, and Cumberland County Library System’s STAR service for homebound senior citizens.

In the following decades, libraries continued to strive to become more accessible. In the 1990s the Library Services and Technology Act and state efforts such as Gov. Tom Ridge’s Link-to-Learn initiative addressed the digital divide between communities that had computers and internet connections and those that did not. It provided grants for libraries to acquire needed upgrades.

Thirty years later, there are still some places in Pennsylvania, especially in rural and mountainous areas, that don’t have broadband. However, that number shrinks each year thanks to federal and state efforts to build infrastructure in communities that corporate entities have neglected.

Some commentators argue that the internet, online databases and AI have replaced the need for public libraries and professional librarians. But a lot of information and recreational reading material is locked behind paywalls that Google and chatbots cannot circumvent.

Librarians today continue to play a crucial role in ensuring that resources remain available to the “largest number, at the least cost,” as American librarian Melvil Dewey articulated more than a century ago.

The Pennsylvania Library Association has found that for every $1 in tax investment, libraries return $5.50 in benefits . This is largely by acquiring materials at discounts and enabling library customers to share and reuse them.

Working in today’s libraries can require substantial courage, too, given current censorship trends in public libraries , including book bans . Requests to remove titles, or reshelve them in less-accessible areas, is nothing new. For example, I documented an example in Scranton in 1898 in which Catholic citizens urged the removal of Augusta Jane Evans-Wilson’s novel “Inez: A Tale of the Alamo,” due to its negative portrayal of a priest and inaccurate descriptions of Catholic sacraments. However, current activists’ tactics are becoming more broad-stroke, aggressive and even violent.

The American Library Association and EveryLibrary , a library advocacy group, have noted bills in various states that propose jailing library employees for the materials their institutions contain. There do not seem to be any bills presently of concern in Pennsylvania. But news reports about other book challenges and bans in Pennsylvania, especially in school libraries , regularly show up in my inbox and social media feeds.

When you view the centuries-long history of American librarianship through a Pennsylvania lens, it’s more complex, nuanced and fascinating than many people realize. And while today’s libraries face various challenges, I believe they continue to contribute enormously to residents across the entire state.
Read more of our stories about Philadelphia and Pennsylvania , or sign up for our Philadelphia newsletter on Substack .
Bernadette A. Lear is a member of the American Library Association and the Pennsylvania Library Association.

articles.title: To crack the job market, internships can be just as key for young people as the degree
articles.author:
<name>Matthew J. Mayhew, Professor of Higher Education, The Ohio State University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/matthew-j-mayhew-206389"/>
paras: College students are facing one of the most precarious labor markets in years. A recent New York Federal Reserve study pointed to a sharp increase in the post-college unemployed compared with other workers, with explanations ranging from artificial intelligence job displacement to a broader slowdown in hiring.

One response has been a boom in trade-school and apprenticeship programs that launch young people into “AI-proof” careers. But students at community and four-year colleges can also beat these headwinds and launch a career through on-the-job internships.

We’re a group of multidisciplinary scholars at The Ohio State University who study two paid internship programs in science, technology, engineering and math, or STEM, with a proven record of landing jobs for students. Although the two initiatives use different models, they both illustrate four lessons that colleges and employers can use to turn internships into genuine career pathways.

Just as notable is that a large share of these students come from diverse and underrepresented backgrounds, with many being the first in their families to go to college. These programs can serve as a powerful equalizer for young people who may not otherwise have such career opportunities.

Internships remain one of higher education’s most powerful tools for preparing students for work. Decades of research show that students who complete high-quality internships are more likely to secure job interviews and high-earning positions post-graduation.

At the same time, the number of internship opportunities is diminishing, even though that preparation matters more than ever. Artificial intelligence is transforming entry-level work , leading employers to increasingly value the human skills that machines cannot easily replicate: judgment, adaptability, collaboration and the ability to solve unfamiliar problems.

Academic leaders are recognizing these pressures. More than one-third of university presidents and two-thirds of community college presidents told an Inside Higher Ed survey that they plan to add or expand apprenticeship pathways over the next three years.
But it’s not just the number of internships that matters – internship quality counts just as much.

Our research at the College Impact Laboratory examined learning through experience with two multi-institutional studies. One is Bridging Academic Training Through Experiential Research and Innovation, or BATTERI , led by principal investigator Jay Sayre and project manager Joanna Gardner . The other is Drive to Thrive .

Across both initiatives, students benefited when their experiences combined substantive work with mentoring and professional development, rather than being treated as inexpensive labor. This distinction suggests that merely placing students in workplaces isn’t enough. The structure and quality of those experiences help determine whether internships lead to meaningful, high-earning careers.

Drive to Thrive deploys an approach called earn-as-you-learn. Through partnerships with Ford dealerships, students alternate between classroom instruction and paid workplace experience. They work alongside experienced technicians, diagnose and repair customers’ vehicles and receive regular coaching.
In this sense, it’s similar to the European model of traineeships for young people.

This initiative reached 635 students at 18 community colleges, including 345 first-generation students and 300 students of color. Through interviews and focus groups, a majority told us the internship helped them see themselves as true professionals. And several said the internship confirmed they had chosen the right career.
The numbers also backed up our approach. Students in the earn-as-you-learn program were almost 50% more likely to graduate compared with students in a matched comparison group.

Our other program brings together clean energy manufacturing students from three different types of institutions – a major research university, a historically Black university and a community college – for a 10-week internship. The program combines workplace learning with professional development workshops, peer networking, community engagement and projects with industry partners such as Honda, Stellantis and Schaeffler.

This initiative took a distinctive approach by assigning multiple mentors to each student. The idea is to help students develop relationships with faculty members, technical experts, employers and classmates. This network, in turn, strengthened students’ confidence, professional identity and sense of belonging while complementing the technical skills they develop.

To date, the formula has worked. More than half the participants in 2025 have already lined up either a new internship or job interviews. Industry partners also plan to rehire several members of the 2026 cohort as interns, extending their training beyond our program and opening pathways into clean-tech careers.

Based on this record, we believe that colleges should build broader support networks around internships rather than expect a single supervisor to shoulder the entire responsibility for a student’s professional development.
In both programs, four valuable principles emerged.

First is the importance of meaningful work. We believe interns should tackle real organizational challenges with deliverables that matter beyond the classroom. For example, two interns spent the summer addressing a safety challenge for Honda – how to prevent battery cells from catching fire and cooling them down when they do.

After developing potential solutions, they presented their work to industry representatives. A senior engineer from the Honda Research Institute was so impressed that he contacted them about a post-internship opportunity.
That sense of consequence changed how the students approached the work. Rather than viewing it as an assignment to complete, they were making a contribution that others depended on.

Second is the constellation of support for students. The liaison between the institution and industry partners is essential, serving as the connective tissue that holds the internship together and ensuring that students don’t fall through the cracks.

But that liaison alone isn’t enough. Students also need access to faculty, industry supervisors, technical experts and peers, since each brings a different kind of guidance. One strength of the clean energy program, for example, is its inclusion of industry experts across institutions and organizations. Students benefit most when they can draw on multiple mentors and peer support to develop key collaborative skills.

Third, students should learn how to normalize struggle. Internships aren’t a test of whether students can already function as professionals. They’re environments for students to try, fail and retry. When educators emphasize struggle as part of the learning process, students are encouraged to avoid perfectionism and instead ask for help when difficulties arise.

For example, students submit weekly reports during the clean energy program that give them the chance to discuss challenges, troubleshoot problems together and recognize that uncertainty is part of becoming a professional.

Finally, it’s vital to make interns’ contributions visible. Presentations, project showcases and recognition from industry professionals reinforce that students’ work matters while strengthening their professional identities.

We believe universities and industries alike should heed these lessons, which extend well beyond clean energy manufacturing and automotive technology. Successful programs build ecosystems that often determine whether students simply complete an internship or launch a career.

As colleges respond to changing labor markets, they should resist measuring success just by how many internships they create. Instead, they should ask whether those opportunities help students become confident, capable professionals. Internship quantity opens the door to better outcomes after college. Internship quality changes lives.

articles.title: No, AI systems don’t have a drive to survive – a developmental psychologist explains why it only looks that way
articles.author:
<name>Peter J. Marshall, Professor of Psychology and Neuroscience, Temple University</name>
      <foaf:homepage rdf:resource="https://theconversation.com/profiles/peter-j-marshall-2485519"/>
paras: In controlled safety tests described earlier this year, researchers asked AI models to solve a series of simple math problems. Partway through the exercise, the instructors warned the bots that if they tried to solve the next problem, the computer environment they were operating in would be shut down. In some runs, the shutdown occurred as specified. In others, models interfered with the shutdown script and continued with the remaining problems.
What explains this behavior? Do artificial intelligence systems have a drive to survive?

Consider a robot vacuum cleaner. When it detects that its battery is running low, it returns to its charger, recharges itself, then resumes cleaning. The machine is keeping itself going, but no one is panicking about an existential Roomba threat to humankind because the behavior is straightforward. Designers built in the ability to recharge.

AI models are more complex. For years, researchers have discussed scenarios in which an AI agent might act to prevent shutdown so it could complete the tasks it had been assigned. Staying “on” could be a means to an end, even without an explicit instruction to resist shutdown.

One recent experiment showed that when researchers spelled out to an AI agent that allowing a shutdown took priority over completing a task, the resistance disappeared. But another, much broader experiment found some resistance even when the researchers instructed the models that allowing a shutdown had priority. Why some resistance remained is an open question.

Self-protective behavior in an AI model may look like a drive to survive. Historian Yuval Noah Harari argued in a recent interview with The Economist that “the first thing that basically any entity learns as it develops is to survive.” He also said that evolution drives organisms toward survival. In a different article, he called survival “ the most basic goal of any agent .”

But does invoking evolution explain why machines or even living things behave in self-preserving ways? A rabbit running from a fox is trying to save itself, and this kind of behavior has likely been favored in evolution. But natural selection is a historical process through which characteristics that contribute to survival and reproduction become more common across generations. It does not give an individual rabbit an instruction to “stay alive.”
Even if AI systems were eventually subject to a comparable process of selection, that alone would not tell us what continued operation means for an individual system.

A rabbit fleeing a fox and an AI altering a shutdown script can look broadly similar: Both behaviors help the individual or system continue. But what it means to continue is not the same in each case.

When a rabbit is not running for its life, it is constantly engaged in breathing, digesting, regulating its temperature, repairing tissue and defending against infection. This ongoing work is more than simple maintenance; it also builds and replaces the structures that make these processes possible. The gut lining that absorbs the rabbit’s food is itself rebuilt, every few days, from the food it absorbs.

The rabbit is alive only as long as this continual producing, maintaining and repairing continues. Staying alive is not the outcome of that activity; it is the activity itself continuing. The rabbit’s existence depends on this ongoing activity, whether or not it is facing an immediate threat.

An AI system may take steps to stay on. In the safety tests, the models did not rewrite their own code or hack into the operating system – they simply moved or renamed the shutdown script, changed its permission or replaced it with something harmless. When that succeeded, the call that was supposed to trigger shutdown didn’t happen, and the model could continue with the task.

But staying on is not the same as staying alive. The shutdown resistance did not lead to a new course of action aimed at keeping the AI model operating. It just helped the model continue the task at hand.

Nor is being switched off the same as dying. For a living organism, death is the irreversible breakdown of the activity that keeps it going. As Harari acknowledged in the Economist interview, “it is not clear what death means for an AI.”

The current shutdown tests show that an unfinished task can be enough to produce shutdown resistance in an AI. Although this behavior is not fully understood, it should not be automatically interpreted as self-preservation.

Whether AI could ever develop anything comparable to the self-producing and self-maintaining organization of living systems is a separate question. Current AI systems are kept running by an engineered infrastructure around them. Their own activity does not continually produce and replace the structures that keep them running.
Shutdown resistance in AI may still be dangerous, but these behaviors do not show that an AI system has a drive to survive.

articles.title: ‘The entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we just live in it’: why the incredible actor broke Emmy records
articles.author: Stuart Heritage
paras: The star of Widow’s Bay is that rarest of talents – someone who can do whatever he wants and make it utterly believable. No wonder he just made TV history

On Monday night, Matthew Rhys made history. He is now officially the first actor ever to win Emmy awards for lead roles in all three categories: drama, comedy and limited series. To make things even more extraordinary, he won two of those awards in a single night.

In the comedy category, Rhys won best lead for Widow’s Bay , the superlative Apple comedy horror where he stars as an indecisive mayor whose island suddenly plays host to a supernatural haunting. He also won best lead actor in a limited series or anthology for The Beast in Me , the Netflix drama about a property developer who may (or may not, no spoilers) have murdered his wife. Add this to his 2018 win for The Americans and the trifecta is complete. In other words, the entire world belongs to Matthew Rhys, and we’re all just living in it.

Kesha sang Old Flames (Can’t Hold a Candle to You), a single her mother wrote for the country music titan. articles.title: Rob Saka Throws Together Traffic Safety Legislation Ahead of Council Deadline
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: Seattle Council transportation committee chair Rob Saka has been rushing forward a set of bills intended to improve traffic safety outcomes on city streets, hoping to beat a legislative deadline before this fall's budget season. The package, which consists of three separate bills , purports to give the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT) additional tools to implement safety upgrades, asks for recommendations around timelines to remediate city streets following fatal crashes, and sets the City up to be able to mandate side guards on vehicles used by city contractors.
However, SDOT has confirmed with The Urbanist that the department was not fully looped in on the package's development, with Saka moving things forward on a very compressed timeline.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Saka rolled out his proposal , which he is calling the Seattle SAFER (Safe Accountable Flexible Equitable Responsive) Streets Act, two days before Mayor Katie Wilson signed an executive order that deals with many of the same topics. Saka, due to his role as committee chair, had reportedly received a briefing on the contents of that executive order, but did not appear at Wilson's press event to roll it out in Beacon Hill on August 21.
The overlap between the new executive order and Saka's legislative proposal is particularly pronounced when it comes to potential regulations around side guards and other vehicle safety retrofits.

"I suppose great minds can arrive at some of the same intersections as we appear to have done and aligned on from a legislative and executive perspective, and that's a good thing," Saka said last week, at the second committee meeting held to discuss the bills. "The two efforts are complementary, but distinct. Executive action can move quickly, [and] initiate changes today. Legislation, by comparison, can establish durable requirements that survive changes in administrations, department leadership, or priorities."

When Saka made those comments, all three of the bills remained in draft form, having missed a prior deadline for introduction and referral before the Council's August recess. Holding a committee discussion, much less two, around a draft version of a bill is unusual, and during last week's meeting several issues surfaced that conveyed how rushed the process has been thus far, including the fact that modifications recommended by the City's law department had been made between the August 20 and September 8 meeting.
So what would the SAFER Streets Act actually do?

The first bill in the package adjusts the authority of the SDOT Director, giving that position explicit authority to do many things that are already under their control. That includes the authorization (not requirement) "to ensure capital project reviews are informed by safety needs identified in a Vision Zero Plan when changes to the configuration or operations of an intersection are proposed and when geography and budget allow." It would codify a requirement that the Vision Zero Plan (which appears to be the same as a Vision Zero Action Plan) be updated every three years.

It would also ask SDOT for a report, to be delivered by next June, that considers options for "improving the Department's existing response following a qualifying fatal crash." That work would build on an internal SDOT policy, adopted in May, that codifies expectations around how the department reviews fatal crashes on city right-of-way, with a two to four-week review after SDOT receives a crash report from the Seattle Police Department and a 90-day timeframe for "remediation or maintenance activities."

That internal policy also includes a twice-yearly review of all crashes involving people who were walking, rolling, biking, or using a scooter or motorcycle. That data is used to inform Vision Zero investments with a goal of making safety upgrades within two years of that review.

Saka's bill asks for at least three "progressively more stringent options" for post fatal crash review, including a requirement to evaluate what it would look like to conduct a review within 72 hours of receiving a crash report, and the potential for remediation to take place within two weeks. Presumably this report would be used to inform future legislation, but the bill ultimately doesn't make any direct changes to city policies around post-crash review.

That bill also includes a section dealing with the amount of time that the Washington State Department of Transportation (WSDOT) spends reviewing potential modifications to highway on and off-ramps within the city, requesting design feedback be returned "within a reasonable amount of time, but in no case more than 180 days." But the City of Seattle has no legal standing to require any specific timelines from another level of government, turning the section into a pretty please.

The second bill in the package addresses the city position of City Traffic Engineer, a position that has been held by Venu Nemani since 2021. Nemani also holds the title of Chief Transportation Safety Officer, after being "elevated" to that role in 2023 following the release of a "top to bottom" review of the department's Vision Zero program.

The bill would not codify that Chief Transportation Safety Officer position, but rather give the City Traffic Engineer explicit authority to do things that are already commonplace, like the ability to "review and provide recommendations to enhance the safety of roadways and transportation infrastructure." It's not clear that a lack of these specific authorities is inhibiting the department from being able to make safety interventions now, and nothing in the bill would require the City Traffic Engineer to do anything differently.

The third bill, which was only discussed conceptually at the August 20 transportation committee meeting, would request requirements for vehicles operated by city contractors to have "truck lateral protective devices," commonly referred to as truck side guards. Placed along the undercarriage of a vehicle, side guards can prevent people who are walking or rolling from being pulled under the vehicle in the event of a crash.
The bill specifically calls out Boston, which codified truck side guard requirements into city code in 2014, and asks for recommendations by May 1 of next year.

During last week's meeting, members of the council's independent central staff raised issues that came from the Department of Finance and Administrative Services (FAS), which would be tasked with implementing the bill – noting that department wasn't looped in until early September.

"We were able to speak with FAS about this bill last week. Very grateful to them for jumping in and providing their analysis," legislative analyst Ann Gorman said. "They raised a couple issues which we have flagged as policy considerations. FAS may require additional resources to develop the requested recommendations. For instance, FAS does not have mechanical engineering capacity, and FAS may not have capacity to perform and/or oversee the requested body of work by the date that is currently in the ordinance."

Wilson's executive order also directed FAS to work on side guards and other potential safety enhancements for contracted vehicles, but instead asks for a report on opportunities and impacts by next January.

"The executive order is very much in a similar subject area, but it is asking for another thing," Gorman said. "It seems reasonable to expect that after the requested report is delivered [...] the mayor's office might consider developing actual requirements about what it has heard based on the opportunity and impact analysis, but that is not what it is doing."

Other members of the transportation committee, including Alexis Mercedes Rinck and Eddie Lin, have raised concerns about the fact that SDOT has not been at the table at any of the committee meetings so far.

"I would be interested in hearing SDOT's feedback, and just want to make sure that – not that we have to adopt what they say – but I do just want to make sure that this is going to work for them as well, and if there are potential concerns or tweaking of anything, that I'd like to have the time to bring those forward for discussion," Lin said.

SDOT press secretary Ethan Bergerson confirmed via email late last week that the department was only looped in on Saka's package on August 19, the day before the first committee discussion was held. SDOT did provide feedback on the bill on September 4, Bergerson said, but no changes were incorporated by the September 8 meeting when Saka assured his colleagues that no further changes would be made. The Urbanist has not yet confirmed the substance of SDOT's feedback.

Councilmembers raised other process concerns. Because the bills aren't set to be formally introduced until September 15, two days before a final committee vote, the deadline to submit amendments was last week. That means councilmembers will have not seen a final version of the bill when being asked to submit potential changes.
"I've never seen an amendment deadline for a piece of legislation that has not formally been introduced yet. How is that possible?" Rinck, the committee's vice chair, asked staff last week.
"I can only tell you that we've been working out how to make all of the pieces fit, and this is the timeline that we've developed to achieve this vote date," was the reply from analyst Amanda Allen.

Saka defended the process to develop the package, and the fact that SDOT has not been at the table for committee discussions, stating that it is common for departments to not be directly involved in meetings on proposals that originate from the legislative branch.

"My office has been working closely with SDOT on this, especially [over] the last six weeks plus, even before that, on various higher-level aspects of this," Saka said. "They have reviewed and provided my office with extensive feedback, and my office has met directly with the department, and the executive, the mayor's office, on our complimentary efforts numerous times. And I would encourage you, Councilmember Lin, vice chair [Rinck] as well, anyone, to meet directly with the department yourselves."

A final committee vote is tentatively scheduled for this Thursday, September 17. If that vote isn't taken, the package would likely be held until the council wraps up its budget work around Thanksgiving.

articles.title: La Dive adds Chiew Chiew by Sugar Hill, a Pike and Pine pairing of wine, Thai street food and bar snacks
articles.author: CHS Staff
paras: Capitol Hill natural wine bar La Dive is pairing Pike and Pine as it turns to a neighbor for help in the kitchen. The hook-up brings easy access to great food at La Dive while also showcasing the creations of an under appreciated neighborhood Thai joint.
The E Pike wine and bubbly night spot is launching Chiew Chiew by Sugar Hill , a new culinary collaboration with the Thai street food restaurant and lounge from just around the corner on E Pine.

Guests at La Dive can order Thai street food and Asian bar snacks like dumplings, noodles, rice dishes, and fries from their tables via QR code with dishes delivered lickety split from Sugar Hill’s kitchen just a block and then some away. The route from the E Pine Thai joint to La Dive is just over 1,000 feet.

The Pike and Pine partnership unites three female entrepreneurs: La Dive co-owners Kate Opatz and Anaïs Custer alongside Sugar Hill owner Guitar Srisuthiamorn . Designed to support women-owned neighborhood businesses amid a challenging hospitality landscape, the concept pairs natural wines and frozen cocktails with a full food menu in what is hoped to be a mutually beneficial experience for the ventures — and for customers.

Now a veteran of the Capitol Hill hospitality scene, Opatz has been increasingly vocal about the real challenges of running a successful restaurant and bar business in the neighborhood and a champion of women nightlife entrepreneurs. One of the latest projects she has boosted is the soon to open “ agave spirit forward ” Bar Laa from first-time owner Laara Garcia in a former Opatz space on E Olive Way.

Sugar Hill debuted in 2016 in the one-time Bauhaus and Capitol Club space but really hit its stride with a refocus on dining coming out of the pandemic in 2021 . “We dumbed down our food when we first came. Here I try to create a menu where it’s gonna be spicy, but we use authentic ingredients and make it taste like home,” Srisuthiamorn said at the time. “I love all the food that comes out. They’re my favorite dishes that I grew up with. I want people to come in and taste what we have to offer that’s not watered down Thai food.”
La Dive, meanwhile, was born in 2019 and has settled in as a dark and cozy hangout featuring a mix of affordable and interesting natural wine and bubbly pours plus a bottle shop.

Chiew Chiew by Sugar Hill runs every night at La Dive with the exception of Mondays which feature guest chef pop-ups. Sugar Hill continues its own operations on E Pine as well, featuring late-night food and live DJ sets Thursday through Saturday.
Visit La Dive at 721 E Pike. Learn more at ladiveseattle.com .
You can find Sugar Hill at 414 E Pine. Learn more at sugarhillseattle.com .

articles.title: Midnight-movie evangelists want to revive Capitol Hill’s historic Egyptian Theatre
articles.author: Justin Carder
paras: A Classified Cinema screening at The Egyptian this summer (Image: Classified Cinema)

A group of midnight movie champions and lovers of physical media are finalizing a lease agreement with property owner Seattle College to reopen the Egyptian Theatre on Capitol Hill. The E Pine venue closed two years ago due to a major pipe burst in the more than 110-year-old former Masonic Temple, followed by SIFF’s decision not to renew its 10-year lease in 2025.
WFLM Seattle , led by Ben Redder alongside Elias Savage, Scotty Wright, and Lanna Hed , is lined up to become a long-term tenant in the theater, The Stranger reports .
Redder brings local cinephile experience having managed Seattle Cinerama and worked at Scarecrow Video , The Stranger notes.

WFLM has been part of a summer of pop-ups and events in the Egyptian as Seattle Central opened a schedule of one-time showings and special screenings to light the theater back up after a long closure following the water pipe break and the exit of SIFF. Meanwhile, the school has been looking for a new long-term tenant for the theater that has been showcasing arthouse, classic, and international cinema since 1980.

The WFLM group has been testing the cinematic waters at the Egyptian with events this summer including a sold-out screening of a documentary on Lenny Wilkens and “secret movie” collaborations and “physical media swaps” for film geeks with Classified Cinema .

“A show there wouldn’t have been possible without volunteers and Seattle Central College,” the group said after a June event at the Egyptian. “Thank you. We fucking love movies (WFLM) and Classified Cinema want to screen more movies and maybe even eventually secure a consistent location.”

According to Redder’s conversation with the Stranger, the group plans to operate the theater similarly to Santa Ana’s Frida Cinema with programming centering on repertory cinema, crowd favorites, forgotten titles, and the return of late-night midnight movie screenings. Redder reports that the building requires minor cosmetic updates, paint, and equipment checks before opening, with organizers targeting operations to begin before the end of the year once the contract is signed and announced.

While Capitol Hill’s golden era with multiple art house film destinations has long passed, recent times have brought some lively new options for the neighborhood’s film communities. CHS reported here on monthly Quality Film Club screenings inside the neighborhood’s old supermarket on 15th Ave E.

Meanwhile, the Northwest Film Forum has held on in its 12th Ave home in the building once home to the Klineburger Brothers taxidermists and neighboring the fortress-like East Precinct , that has been part of real estate investor and arts supporter Elizabeth Linke’s 12th Ave holdings.
On E Pine, Seattle Central tells CHS it “is in talks with an organization to use the Egyptian Theatre” but said the lease is not yet signed.

articles.title: Washington’s Republican News Site Gets Money from the Conservative Group Funding Anti-Trans Initiatives
articles.author: John Stang
paras: Two people financing efforts to stop a millionaires’ income tax and to ban transgender girls from girls’ sports are also financially backing the Center Square, a conservative national news operation with Washington State reporters covering those same measures.

Let’s Go Washington has three measures on November’s ballot—to repeal a new state millionaires’ income tax, to ban trans girls from girls sports, and to modify student privacy rights in schools. Let’s Go Washington is led by Redmond hedge fund manager Brian Heywood; one of the organization’s top five donors is trucking executive Steve Gordon, according to Let’s Go Washington’s website.
Gordon and Heywood are the chairman and vice chairman of Project 42, a political action committee they founded to fund conservative ventures across Washington and elsewhere.

Between 2021 and 2024, the Chicago-based Franklin News Foundation, parent organization to the Center Square, was the top recipient of Project 42 funds. According to philanthropy.org, a nationwide donation-tracking website, it gave $3.1 million. It’s unclear how much of that money went toward the Center Square’s operation in Washington state, but during those four years, Project 42 was the Franklin News Foundation’s second biggest donor, about $800,000 shy of the conservative Donor’s Trust.

In 2024, the same year that Project 42 had four initiatives on the ballot, it donated $1.2 million to the Franklin News Foundation for “media investigative reporting.” (Only one initiative, which forbade the state from banning natural gas, passed.) That was the first year that Let’s Go Washington had initiatives on a state ballot.

What that money partly funds is the Center Square, a publication which concentrates on tax and business matters, but stretches into other political issues such as trans girls participating in girls sports. It opened its Washington operation in 2021, the same year that Project 42 was created. Project 42 acknowledges the Center Square as an ally on its website. The years after its founding, Project 42 donated more than $798,60035 in 2022 and $825,840 in 2023 to the Franklin foundation, according to influencewatch.org. No figures were available for 2021, 2025, and 2026.

“Donors don’t shape our coverage,” Center Square and Franklin News Foundation CEO Chris Krug wrote in an email to The Stranger . Federal regulations allow the Franklin News Foundation to keep donors’ identities confidential. Krug did not answer a question about the size of the Center Square’s budget for Washington state.
Heywood and a Project 42 spokesman did not return requests for comments.

While their donors may not shape coverage, perhaps the opinions and beliefs of the Center Square’s reporters do. At least, that’s what the Washington State Attorney General’s Office thinks. The Center Square and Attorney General Nick Brown’s office recently crossed swords over the non-work online activity of its reporter, TJ Martinell.

Martinell has written Center Square stories critical of the attorney general’s office, including how the office gave legal advice to the Democrats while they put together a millionaires tax; how publicly requested documents were distributed ; and how many attorneys general, including Washington’s Nick Brown, coordinated lawsuits against President Trump before he was re-elected . Martinell also has a virulently racist and misogynic digital footprint that Brown’s office takes issue with.

On July 28, David Postman, Brown’s chief of staff, wrote a long letter to Center Square CEO Chris Krug complaining about Martinell. Postman acknowledged that the attorney general’s office is unhappy with some of Martinell’s coverage. But his letter focused on the reporter’s off-the-job activities, stating they weren’t a good fit with an office with a high number of women and people of color on staff.

“I am alarmed by the writings and comments by Washington State Center Square reporter TJ Martinell on multiple social media channels and blogs. … His stated views point to political biases, racial prejudices, misogyny, and conspiracy theories,” Postman wrote.
Here is a partial list of examples listed in Postman’s letter, which The Stranger has also confirmed.

First, Martinell is one of four co-founders of the Masculine Geek website , the “21st Century men’s club” which is a place for “masculine men to [discuss] history, guns, literature, women, art, or whatever else inspires them.” That may not be all they get up to on there. One Masculine Geek article is a nasty first-person story (Martinell is not the writer) about a man degrading and abusing a woman with whom he was having an affair. It’s not apparent whether the story is fact or fiction.

Second, Martinell made a comment on a Substack post that appears to discuss immigration. Martinell wrote: “Our grandparents didn’t experience the largest human migration in human history. … We have been expected to welcome people into our neighborhoods with 1000x worse intentions than 1942 Imperial Japan or Nazis Germany had for the USA.”

Third, Martinell participates in Old Glory Club functions. The nationwide club is a far-right, antisemitic men’s-only network, according to the Guardian . During a January Old Glory Club podcast , Martinell said:
* He wanted to go to Somalia or another country with emigrants going to the United States—and destroy its people.
* “Trump should be doing what he did to that Venezuela president to foreigners in elected positions in our country.”
*Martinell also said Chicago-born Boston Mayor Michelle Wu has “got Chinese spy written on her.”

* Indian immigrant men should be easy to deport because “they give white women the ick. …They’ve probably interacted with more white women through adult films more than they’ve ever interacted with a woman in real life.”
* Many churches and pastors are “communists” and some men wanting to be ministers are “gamma male mama’s boys.”
* Bad childhoods prompt men to enter interracial marriages. (Attorney General Nick Brown is the child of a mixed-race marriage.)
Martinell did not respond to a request for comment .
On Aug. 10, Krug sent a reply to Brown, stating while he didn’t agree with Martinell’s extracurricular online activity, it didn’t influence his journalism at the Center Square.

“I find much of that (non-Center Square) commentary distasteful and indefensible. And I will make no excuses for any of it,” Krug wrote. He explained that he had discussed this and the fact that “a journalist’s participation in public discussion of contemporary social questions is not cleanly separable from his professional standing” with Martinell. “None of Mr. Martinell’s commentary appeared in the Center Square, and none of it has any bearing on the accuracy of his reporting.”

Krug strongly implied that these complaints are retributive. According to Krug, the attorney general’s office is angry with Martinell’s reporting that it provided legal advice to Democratic legislative leaders on how to write the millionaires’ tax that would withstand the 1933 Washington Supreme Court ruling that’s been routinely used to politically squelch income tax legislation for more than 90 years.

“An office of the State of Washington has now compiled a file on a working reporter. It cataloged his private speech across three years, timestamped to the minute. It transmitted that file to his employer. And it stated, in Mr. Postman’s words, that he struggles ‘with how our office should engage with Martinell given his commentary and rhetoric that is clearly out of bounds for a legitimate reporter,’” Krug wrote. “… It is not the business of the Office of the Attorney General to assemble dossiers on the private views of journalists, to determine which of them is a legitimate reporter.”
Postman wrote that the attorney general’s office will continue to cooperate with Martinell’s future information requests. Krug wrote Martinell will continue to cover the attorney general’s office.

articles.title: Stranger Suggests: Your Agenda This Week, September 14–September 20
articles.author: Julianne Bell, Todd Hamm, Chase Hutchinson, Amanda Manitach, and Nico Swenson
paras: (FOOD & DRINK) Known as “BlackForager” on Instagram and YouTube and “alexisnikole” on TikTok, Alexis Nikole Nelson has charmed millions of followers with her joyful approach to foraged foods, not to mention her sense of humor, adorable forest fairy princess outfits, and fun plant-based recipes. Although her videos are light-hearted, Nelson is serious about foraging: She often delves into the cultural and historical context of the pastime, especially as it relates to Black and Indigenous communities, and she ends many videos with the half-joking warning, “Happy snacking, don’t die!” That catchphrase is also the title of her new debut book, which takes the guesswork and intimidation out of foraging with identification photos, tips, safety information, and seasonal recipes ranging from rosewater baklava to oyster mushroom “chowdah.” Her first book tour stop is at Town Hall and is sure to inspire audience members to scrounge for treats among the natural bounty of the Northwest. ( Town Hall, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL
Tom Barnes: The road goes on forever and the party never ends

(VISUAL ART) He may have been the most 86’ed man in Seattle—a fact that puts a smile on the faces of his closest friends and chosen family. Capitol Hill lost a legend earlier this year, when Tom Barnes departed this earthly plane for the party in the sky. Barnes was well-rounded as a bohemian, in both romantic and problematic ways. Above all, he was an artist and documentarian who painted the world with pure fascination and unbridled pleasure. As a barfly and resident artist at Cha Cha Lounge, he documented the characters and tipplers passing through, rendering figures in big, inky, explosive color and scribbly scrawl that somehow marries on the page to communicate something like pure, incandescent poet energy. Barnes left behind over 800 works of art; come visit the retrospective and raise a glass to the legend. ( Vermillion ) AMANDA MANITACH
Queer Sick Pay Fund Presents: Suns Out, Ones Out

(PERFORMANCE) Seattle does a great job of supporting queer artists, but end-stage capitalism does not. That’s where fundraising can help, and this one is packed with talent! Suns Out, Ones Out raises money for the Queer Sick Pay Fund (qSPF), an organization that provides sick pay to queer, contracted performers when they need to miss a gig due to illness. qSPF has also begun offering gender-affirming care grants for the greater Seattle area. Even if your goal wasn’t to donate to such an awesome cause, you’d still want to go just to catch the show! Featuring drag, music, and comedy, the lineup includes Moscato Sky, Taylar Elizza Beth, CHAD, Emma Schmuckler, DJ dark wiley, and qSPF co-founder, Betty Wetter. The evening will also include a silent auction, raffle, and raise the paddle. Who doesn’t like a good paddling?! ( Clock-Out Lounge, 8:30 pm, 21+ ) NICO SWENSON

(PERFORMANCE) The Kings are back in town! Summoning a whopping 60 performers from drag scenes across North America, this annual festival enters its fourth year with a jaw-dropping, swoon-worthy, swashbuckling explosion of brilliant entertainment. Rusty Hammer is on the bill, and I have a crush on his five-o’clock shadow alone. The festivities span three days of vendors, headliners, featured local talent, and a fierce competition for the ultimate title of High King Supreme. My favorite thing is when they release application statistics as teasers. This year’s top submitted act themes were “gender liberation, religion (the pope), musical theatre, and devils.” Sign me up! ( Broadway Performance Hall, 8 pm, ASL interpreted, 18+ ) NICO SWENSON

From the larger-than-life personas to the homoerotic lore and campy costumes, there’s something about pro wrestling that is just inherently queer, which is why it makes perfect sense that Canadian curator, producer, and performance artist Clayton Lee has chosen it as a backdrop for examining his sexuality. This deeply personal performance marries Lee’s childhood fixation on legendary professional wrestler Bill Goldberg with Bach’s classical compositions known as the Goldberg Variations , resulting in an exploration of power dynamics, desire, and identity. Lee is the artistic director of Fierce Festival in Birmingham, UK and served as the director of the experimental Rhubarb Festival in Canada from 2019–2023, so you can trust him to get real weird with it—the On the Boards website describes the show as “unhinged” and “thoroughly unconventional,” and executive and artistic director Megan Kiskaddon says it “brings toxic relationships to a new level.” ( On the Boards, 7:30 pm ) JULIANNE BELL

(MUSIC) Chelsea Wolfe is at her best when her songs take a turn for the unexpected. See: the shocking rush of tempo change at the end of her 2017 track “Twin Fawn” that could jump-start a car, or the gorgeous, floating-into-the-light arpeggios that bloom amidst the vampirish “Sick” from 2013’s Pain Is Beauty . Something similar happens halfway through the late album slow-burner “Death Is Not the End” from her recent The Dark LP, when a wall of distortion installs itself inside of a quiet moment that, in Wolfe’s world, has become too quiet for comfort. In the absence of such moments that grab hold of the listener, however, Wolfe’s songs have the tendency to meander aimlessly through the still life of her American Gothic scenes, or worse, become predictable. Aside from the above moment, The Dark is her first solo effort (we won’t speak of her Converge collaboration) to fall into such pitfalls, with the added knock of an overly clean production, which saps the caught-in-the-woods allure of her previous recordings. Wolfe’s catalog runs deep, though, so there should still be plenty to be scared by. ( Moore Theatre, 8:30 pm, all ages ) TODD HAMM

(VISUAL ART) What’s not to love about 200-plus artists spread across 20 city blocks of downtown Seattle? It’s free and dog-friendly, too! During last year’s inaugural art marathon, brass bands burst onto the streets, dancers mobilized on rooftops and sidewalks, and videos were projected inside a sunken parking garage. This year, the route is reversed, kicking off in Westlake Park at 11 a.m. and ending at Occidental Square. One caveat: Last year’s wayfinding was a little tricky. If that’s the case again, my advice is to study the route beforehand and plot a path so you don’t miss artists like Dez’Mon Omega Fair, one of my favorite performance artists in town; Charmi Shah, who is hiding collectable, baseball-card-size collages along the route for participants to find and keep; and Jesse Higman, whose interactive paint-pouring technique, performed around a massive tilting table, is mesmerizing. Or just wander blindly and let the art happen to you, because the magic of this event is that you get to experience the city in a completely new way. ( Various locations throughout downtown, 11 am–7:30 pm ) AMANDA MANITACH

(FILM) Local Sightings, Seattle’s most dedicated hyperlocal film festival, is back with a bunch of standout works from local filmmakers you may not have heard of just yet, but absolutely should. One must-see is Marjorie Conrad’s The Joyless Economy , which is making its North American premiere after first screening at the Cannes Film Festival. An experimental documentary about desire, cinema, and a Seattle woman whose life was reshaped by her relationship to the movies, The Joyless Economy is a purposefully challenging, captivating vision. The fest lineup also includes other local gems such as Again Again , Assets & Liabilities , and The Life We Leave , the documentary about local human composting company, Return Home. It proves once more that the Pacific Northwest may often be imitated (eat your heart out, Vancouver), but nobody can replicate the filmmakers themselves. ( Northwest Film Forum, times vary ) CHASE HUTCHINSON

articles.title: Op-Ed: Building Toward a Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle
articles.author: Logan Schmidt
paras: There’s a reason Seattle is called the Emerald City in the Evergreen State: our trees help make Seattle the vibrant city that it is. But preserving that vision doesn’t mean we have to choose between protecting them and building the housing we need. We can – and must – do both.
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

In 2007, Seattle established a goal to reach 30% tree canopy coverage by 2037. At the time, the city’s canopy stood at 18%, according to the City’s Urban Forestry Management Plan . To reach their goal, the City of Seattle Urban Forestry Coalition – consisting of an interdepartmental team of staff from Seattle Parks and Recreation, the Seattle Department of Transportation (SDOT), the Office of Sustainability and the Environment, and more – put forth a list of short and long-term actions, including improving planting and maintenance of City-managed trees, strengthening incentives and regulations to encourage tree preservation on private property, and exploring new financing mechanisms to fund City-operated urban forestry programs.

Seattle has made strong progress toward that goal: the most recent tree canopy study , using data from 2021, has Seattle at 28.1% canopy coverage, an increase of 10 percentage points in 14 years – even as the city’s population grew by nearly 150,000 people and added more than 100,000 new units of housing. As the city prepares for more growth, we have an opportunity to develop new policies and investments to close the remaining gap and meet or even exceed the City’s 30% goal.

And while we continue to care for trees and our environment, Seattle is also grappling with a serious housing shortage. Under the One Seattle Plan ’s adopted growth targets, Seattle must plan for 120,000 new housing units by 2044, or roughly 6,000 homes per year.

Since 2017, Seattle added 8,300 new homes in the Neighborhood Residential (formerly Single Family) zone, typically where detached, ADUs, and moderate middle housing products are built. In lowrise, midrise, highrise, and downtown zones, where apartments are more prevalent, 27,500 units were added. However, data shows a significant downturn in permits in 2025 and 2026, which is a concerning reality for what’s to come, considering new housing takes years to move from permit to construction to occupancy.

The slowing production of housing will only further place strain on homeowners and renters in the city. Seattle homebuyers spent 54.1% of their income on housing costs in 2024, making it one of the least affordable housing markets in the country. And nearly 50% of renter households in the region are cost burdened , meaning they're paying more than 30% of their income on rent.

So, how are we, as a city and region, responding to this pressure? Well, the answer is two-fold. The One Seattle Plan is both Seattle’s Comprehensive Plan – the 20-year vision and roadmap for the city’s growth, required under Washington’s Growth Management Act (GMA) – and the vehicle through which Seattle adopted middle housing: duplexes, triplexes, fourplexes, and other “ missing middle ” housing types mandated statewide by House Bill 1110 . In other words, the same document that guides how Seattle grows responsibly is also the one legalizing more homes in more neighborhoods.

However, the GMA doesn’t just require cities like Seattle to develop comprehensive plans and regulations to guide their growth. It requires local governments to treat housing, transportation, the environment, and more as coequal goals, not competing ones.

Despite this requirement, in public debates at City Hall, goals like more housing and the environment are seemingly – and incorrectly so – pitted against each other. Seattle’s own Urban Forestry Commission has pushed back on the notion that urban density and tree canopy cannot coexist, noting that “what we need to do is better understand how we balance one and the other, while acknowledging that both are necessary.”

Why does the conversation then so often fall into a choice between the two? And instead of asking whether we can have housing or trees, maybe it’s worth asking: what policy choices let us have both ? That starts with recognizing Seattle’s role in the broader region and building on the approaches already showing that density and canopy can grow together.

When cities enact policies that limit opportunities for new housing, that new development doesn't stop – it just moves elsewhere. And that prevents people who want to live and work in a city like Seattle from accessing homes in the transit-oriented, walkable neighborhoods Seattleites and our local government have spent years investing in. Pushing people further out into car-dependent areas results in longer commutes, more vehicle miles traveled, and more emissions. It also means more roads and parking lots replacing permeable land, sending stormwater runoff into local waterways, and further harming our salmon and orca populations .

Furthermore, building new housing in the city can make our current urban environment better. According to a recent King County study of Lake Washington , from 2000 to 2020, the population of the watershed grew by 34% while developed land area grew by less than 5% and forest cover remained steady. Rather than clearing intact forest to accommodate growth, the population grew in place by converting from lower-density to higher-density housing. This new development likely prompted stormwater upgrades, septic-to-sewer transitions, and other changes that helped improve the lake’s water quality.

Not only have we seen improvements in the lake’s water quality, but we’ve also seen new construction lead to planting and protecting trees on site at a rate 325% higher than tree removals are occurring. Since July 2023, when Seattle’s Tree Protection Ordinance went into effect, more than 14,100 trees have been planted and protected during the construction of new homes compared to roughly 4,300 trees removed.

Of those trees removed during construction, nearly 88% were a Tier 3, Tier 4, or below category. The majority of the older, larger tree loss is happening entirely outside of construction: nearly 71% of all Tier 2 tree removals are non-construction-related (Tier 2 trees include trees 24 inches or greater, tree groves, and specific tree species as provided by a Director’s Rule ).

We continue to be interested in finding more ways to preserve and add trees alongside the construction of new housing. However, if protecting Seattle’s most significant trees is the goal, the data points toward paying more attention to the far larger share of removals occurring with no new housing to show for it.

Even worse, and not accounted for in the data above, the largest net change in Seattle’s canopy coverage between 2016 and 2021 occurred in publicly owned parks (“Parks Natural Areas”). Seattle’s parks saw a 5.1% canopy loss, accounting for nearly half of the city’s overall canopy loss (111 of the 255 acres lost) across all management types (neighborhood residential, right-of-way, etc.).

The public right-of-way didn’t fare much better. Over that same period, the city lost 10 acres of canopy in the right-of-way alone – land the city already owns and controls, and the same land that makes up 27% of Seattle’s total area . This points exactly to where the opportunity is: parks and the public right-of-way represent the few places the city can take action on to impact canopy growth directly.

Everyone who cares about housing and trees needs to continue to work on creative solutions for both. Many of our members continue to do that and we look forward to hearing new ideas. In the meantime, we already have solutions we can start implementing now. If new housing isn’t the leading culprit for Seattle’s canopy loss, then we should be putting less energy into pitting homebuilding against trees amidst a regional housing shortage. Rather, it’s time to get serious about growing canopy everywhere. Seattle’s already set the target: 30% canopy by 2037. Getting there means treating tree planting like the public priority it actually is.
Here’s are strategies we can start implementing now:

None of this requires choosing between a growing city and a green one – the data backs that up, and the Complete Communities Coalition laid out the case in more detail in their fact sheet, Right Tree, Right Place: A Greener, Housing-Abundant Seattle .

Jesse Simpson (he/him) is the Director of Government Relations and Policy for the Housing Development Consortium. Jesse grew up in West Seattle and has lived in Capitol Hill since 2018.

Jeff Paul (they/he) is Co-Executive Director of House Our Neighbors, an organization dedicated to housing affordability and climate action that advocates and mobilizes to realize social housing for the residents of Seattle and beyond.

articles.title: “Hop On Board!” Campaign Kicks Off
articles.author: Nathan Dickey
paras: Yesterday, a coalition of transit advocates launched “Hop On Board!”, the official campaign urging Seattle voters to pass the renewal and expansion of the Seattle Transit Measure this November . Speakers at the event included Seattle Mayor Katie Wilson, Councilmember Alexis Mercedes Rinck, ATU 587 President Greg Woodfill, Nondrivers Alliance founder Anna Zivarts, Transit Riders Union General Manager Lam Ho, and Transportation Choices Coalition ‘s Executive Director Kirk Hovenkotter and Policy Director Katy Ricchiuto.

The Transportation Choices Coalition is leading local advocates pushing for expansion of the transit measure, which proposes to increase the current 0.15% sales tax for transit to 0.3%, the maximum allowed under recently adopted state law. If approved by voters, the measure would take effect in April 2027.

King County Metro uses an equity framework to distribute service across King County but cities have the ability to purchase additional service. Seattle has been buying additional service since 2014 , which brought frequent buses to most of the city and dramatically increased the viability of living car-free.

The current Seattle Transit Measure funds over 7% of all bus trips currently running in Seattle, mainly boosting service along key corridors during the day and providing the majority of Metro’s Night Owl service in the city. The expanded STM would further boost service at night and on weekends, as well as more than doubling the number of free ORCA cards for those who need it and providing funding for several important accessibility programs. The measure also includes funding for capital funding for bus lanes.

At the event, speakers shared stories of how important transit is to their lives and how this measure would make public transit in Seattle more useful for more people. Mayor Wilson focused on the importance of late night bus service to help service workers get home at the end of a late shift without using a rideshare service like Uber or Lyft, or making it possible for a family with two cars to only need one.

Councilmember Rinck shared stories of three-seat rides to Tumwater and the importance of frequent, reliable service, and also highlighted the expanded late night service provided by the measure. Greg Woodfill posited that although sales taxes are regressive, this measure’s taxes will go right back to serving the people who need it most, stating “every $1 spent on transit is $5 back in the community”. Anna Zivarts stressed the importantance of frequent and reliable service to those who cannot drive, and how the transit measure would bring more service to more communities. Zivarts put it simply: “transit is freedom”. Other speakers highlighted the proposed increase in free ORCA passes for low-income riders and the elderly, and the importance of pushing back against likely opposition to the measure.
If you are intersested in supporting the Hop On Board campaign, you can sign up to volunteer for upcoming events , or donate to the campaign .

articles.title: Environmental Complaints Against Seattle Growth Plan Thrown Out in State Ruling
articles.author: Ryan Packer
paras: The City of Seattle has some updates to make to the environmental review used to update its 20-year housing and jobs growth plan, but claims alleging that corners were cut when conducting that review were mostly thrown out this week in a ruling from Washington's Growth Management Hearings Board (GMHB).
The Urbanist's Fall Member Drive is in full swing! Support our work, read ad-free, and help us hit our goal for the member drive!

Wednesday's ruling came in response to a set of two appeals filed against the final environmental impact statement (FEIS) for former mayor Bruce Harrell's One Seattle Comprehensive Plan update. The 1,300-page document reviewed impacts from expanding the city's zoning capacity to allow denser development, particularly along transit corridors and in tight clusters close to existing business districts.

These GMHB appeals are separate from the pair of City-level FEIS appeals that have been advancing through the state court system; those are still pending after the Washington Court of Appeals ruled that they should be able to move forward. It's those challenges that are currently holding up implementation of the Comprehensive Plan's second phase, now pushed to at least early 2027.

There is some overlap, however. One of the appeals ruled on this week was filed by Jennifer Godfrey, the Seattle Symphony musician who challenged the FEIS at the city level last year and took her appeal all the way to the Washington Court of Appeals. Godfrey alleged that the plan did not adequately address concerns around the impact of polluted stormwater runoff on Puget Sound's population of Southern Resident killer whales (SRKW). The "Orca Appeal" has attracted significant media attention while Godfrey also pursued this parallel avenue to challenge the FEIS, joined by groups including the Orca Conservatory, the Orca Network, and the Puget Sound Harvesters Association. Collectively that group was referred to as the Joint Petitioners by the hearings board.

Godfrey's appeal argued that the One Seattle Plan sets lofty policies regarding tree canopy preservation and water-quality protection, but that the regulations that are tasked with implementing those policies aren't shown to be in alignment with those policies. But the board ruled that no evidence had been presented to show that this was the case.

"The Board disagrees that it was the City’s burden to show how its implementing regulations ' comply' with its policies," the ruling stated. "Instead, it was Joint Petitioners’ burden to show how the implementing regulations are inconsistent with the policies. But Joint Petitioners did not discuss even a single line of text from the implementing regulations, anywhere in their brief, and so fail to meet their burden."

In issuing its final ruling the board found that Seattle had adequately reviewed the potential impacts of housing growth over the next 20 years, it just didn't encompass enough potential growth. It ultimately ruled the FEIS was inadequate because the City had only reviewed the impacts of what is considered "maximum likely development" instead of "maximum possible development" – a move that leaves out approximately 42,000 potential units of housing based on City planners' estimates.

The City argued that considering the impact of development that is unlikely would be speculative, and thus not required under the State Environmental Policy Act (SEPA) but the growth board did not agree with that either.

"The Board is cognizant of the rule that speculative environmental impacts do not need to be analyzed. It is tempting to think that if additional housing units beyond 120,000 new units are unlikely to be built, then their environmental impacts must be speculative," the ruling said. "That was the logic underlying the City’s decision to limit its environmental analysis to the 120,000 new units it thought were likely under the Update Ordinances, rather than the new development capacity of 162,847 potential new units which the Update Ordinances added to the baseline capacity, or the final capacity of 330,933 potential new units. However, the Board believes that SEPA caselaw distinguishes between impacts that are speculative versus development that is speculative."

During the earlier public comment period, urbanists and housing advocates had raised the point that the City's growth targets appeared on the low side . Divided over 20 years, 120,000 is just 6,000 units added per year, which Seattle has managed to exceed on a regular basis over the recent decade.
But on the underlying environmental analysis for the growth that was studied, the hearings board essentially gave the City its stamp of approval.

"The Board finds that Joint Petitioners have not shown the City failed to use the best available science. The FEIS was deficient for its scope, but not for the quality of the scientific information it relied upon," the ruling stated.

The second GMHB appeal, filed by civil engineer (and past Urbanist contributor ) Donna Breske, dealt with the City of Seattle's plans for water infrastructure, and was fully dismissed. Unlike in Godfrey's appeal, Breske's appeal didn't seek to invalidate any ordinance, but rather force the city to overhaul the Comprehensive Plan's Capital Facilities element to address the current unpredictability of the water permitting process.

The City of Seattle now has a full year to update the One Seattle plan's FEIS to address the potential impacts of the additional units, when it was already in the process of conducting environmental review of even more added density as part of mayor Katie Wilson's pivot from the One Seattle Plan – which has been branded " Taller Denser Faster ."

"[A]s the Board has been at pains to repeat, the FEIS’s environmental analysis would have been adequate [emphasis theirs] if the maximum potential development as a result of the Update Ordinances had been 120,000 new units," the ruling said. "For any amount of growth below this threshold, the FEIS is already adequate . It is only if growth were to exceed the 120,000 new unit threshold that the impacts would not have been considered and mitigated in the FEIS."

The larger issue surrounding Seattle's Comprehensive Plan is what happens with Godfrey's other appeal, which has been moving forward with an appeal filed by Mount Baker resident John M. Cary. Earlier this summer, the Seattle City Council passed a new law that closes off the avenue of appeals to the city hearings examiner when it comes to areawide rezones or updates to the Comprehensive Plan just like this one. That means that it will likely be left to King County Superior Court to adjudicate, with the Council free to consider and adopt the modest rezones that had been on deck before things were put on hold .
While there's no telling how that appeal will ultimately play out, this week's hearings board ruling could provide a preview.
